speechtext: Mr. J. A. CURRIE (East Simcoe) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 59 to amend the Criminal Code.
Explain.

I shall read the Bill,
which will explain itself. It is an amendment to iSection 79 ,of the Criminal Code and reads as follows:
79. A. Any person who votes for any person, for any public officer, or who takes any active part in any election for any public office by becoming a candidate, sneaking, writing, canvassing or driving voters to the poll, who was or is a citizen of any country, now or at any time during the past five years at war with Great Britain or her Allies; or who was a subject of any country not allied with Great Britain or her Allies, which does not permit its citizens the rights of expatriation, or holds the doctrine of dual citizenship or who was exiled or banished from any allied country, even though such person may have been granted naturalization in Canada or Great Britain, or may have his or her name on the Voters' List; shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act, and on conviction before a court of competent jurisdiction shall be liable to imprisonment for a term of not less than two years, together with forfeiture of civil rights and all property to the Crown.
B.	The above provisions shall not apply to any person who is. serving or has served in His Majesty's Forces, or has been a naturalized British subject resident in Canada for twenty-five years. The burden of proof as to such exception shall rest upon the Voter.
C.	Any person giving such information as will lead to the conviction of any such person shall be entitled to one-third of all fines and forfeitures.
I informed the Minister of Finance sometime ago that I intended to introduce this Bill, and he asked me to defer its introduction until the return of the leader of the Government. I have done so, but unfortunately the time for dealing with measures introduced by private members has expired. I would therefore ask the Government to set aside a day to discuss this subject.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

speechtext: In the absence of the Minister of Agriculture I wish to draw the attention of the Prime Minister to a matter that was mentioned a couple * of days ago with regard to action that is alleged to have been taken in connection with the export of the surplus supply of cheese. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PURCHASE OF CHEESE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Owing to the
indisposition of the Minister of Agriculture,, I am not, perhaps, as fully informed as I should be on the subject. I did address a: somewhat urgent communication on the matter two days ago, but I have not yet received a reply. I am under the impression that the British Government have decided to take over at a fixed price all cheese coming either from the United States ot from Canada. This was done some time ago with regard to Australia and New Zealand; ar-rangments were made which were accepted by the governments of these Dominions and by the British Government. The diffl-culty here has been the ascertainment of a proper price. I think that the Commission that was appointed has found itself unable to act so far on account of the difficulty experienced by the British Commissioner in obtaining the necessary instructions from the British Board of Trade. There has been no inaction on the part of this Government, who have been endeavouring to do everything in their power, but as the British Government are to be the purchasers, certain conditions must be authorized by them and cannot be authorized by us. So far as I have gone into the details I have been speaking more from impression than from actual knowledge, and my. remarks must be taken subject to that qualification. I have, however, given an accurate statement of the situation so far as I have knowledge of it at the moment., I shall inquire from the Minister of Agriculture whether he can, give any additional information on the subject.	*

House of Commons, May 31, 1917.
The special committee, appointed to consider and report upon the arrangements which should be made for the celebration of the fiftieth anniversary of the foundation of this Dominion, ask leave to submit the following recommendations as their first and final report.
That a topical pamphlet comparing and contrasting Canada of 1867 with Canada of 1917, be published for the purpose of drawing attention to the outstanding features of Canadian growth and development and giving direction to the thoughts which should animate the memorial services.
That the Government issue a proclamation Inviting churches, Sabbath and day schools, *colleges, municipal authorities, Canadian Clubs and other associations to co-operate in the working out of fitting corhmemorative services for the day.
That the Provincial authorities be requested to arrange for a special official celebration of the anniversary at the capitals of the several provinces.
That the Federal Government provide for the issuance of a commemorative post card andi postage stamp, with appropriate design and legend representative of the work of the Fathers of Confederation.
That appropriate memorial services be held at London and Paris on July 1st.
That upon the central stone column, upholding the roof of the great entrance hall of the new Parliament buildings, the following inscription be incised:

1867	 1917 !

That all the words after "that" in the main motion be struck out, and the following substituted therefor:
"Inasmuch as cotton jute, or paper sacks, when containing flour, now enter Canada from the United States free of duty, and inasmuch as Canadian millers employing Canadian labour are handicapped because they are compelled to pay on empty sacks and bags, a duty of 27|% on cotton and jute bags and sacks, and a duty of 35% on paper sacks. This House is of the opinion that such unfair discrimination should be removed, therefore it is resolved that in the opinion of this House, cotton and jute bags

and sacks and paper sacks, when imported by millers for use in their own mills should be free of duty."
He said:	Mr. Speaker, the amendment
of mine which you ruled out of order was of greater importance to my constituents than that which I now move, and I would have much preferred had the Houee had an opportunity of discussing that amendment. Had I 'been considering my own business alone, perhaps I should not be so strongly in favour of free 'bran and shorts; but representing an agricultural constituency as I do, where the supplies of bran and shorts are used for the production of milk, cream, butter and cheese, and having in view the interest of producers in these lines throughout the country, I submit the present resolution. Owing to the recent Order in Council conditions are rapidly arising under which the farmers, especially those of eastern Canada, will be compelled to pay much more for their feedstuffs than they should pay. This resolution is necessary because in the revision of the United States tariff, the so-called Underwood tariff, included clause 644, which names certain articles a.s on the free list. That clause is as follows:
Wheat, wheat flour, semolina, and other wheat products not specially provided for in this section. Provided, That wheat shall be subject to a duty of ten cents per bushel, that wheat flour shall be subject to a duty of 45 cents per barrel of 196 pounds; and seminola and other products of wheat, not specially provided for in this section, 10 per centum ad valorem, when imported directly or indirectly, from a country, dependency, or other subdivision of government, which imposes a duty on wheat or wheat flour or semolina imported from the United States.
This clause means that Canadian wheat is subject to a duty of ten cents a bushel on entering the markets of the United States, unless Canada accepts a proposition prepared in Washington without consulting Ottawa, a proposition altogether different from the much-abused Fielding-Knox proposition of 1911. It gives United States millers special privileges in the Canadian markets, privileges which, in my judgment, will ultimately result in reduced production of flour in this country, and consequently reduced production of the bran and shorts so necessary for the farmers of eastern Canada. Under the proposition of 1911 precaution was taken not to interfere in any way with manufacturing in Canada, and especially was this precaution taken with Tespeet to our milling industry, for a duty of fifty cents a barrel on flour was provided, which enabled the Canadian millers, in a measure, to offset the increased cost of bags

in Canada as compared with the United States. The Canadian miller had a protection of fifty cents a barrel in a market that was growing at the rate of one new flour mill of a thousand barrels a day every year, and consequently there was a steadily increasing production of bran and shorts. It may be interesting for the House to know that while in 1895 Canada exported less than 250,000 barrels of flour, in 1910 our exports reached 3,000,000 barrels, and in 1915-16, 7,426,000 barrels. _
In taking the position that the recent Order in Council will be injurious to Canadian millers, and consequently will lessen the supply of bran and shorts for the stock feeders of Canada, I am in good company. On reference to Hansard of 1916, I find that in the debate on a resolution presented by my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), which was opposed by the Government, the Finance Minister (Sir Thomas White) expressed about the same views on. this question as I do. I may say quite frankly, I was never very much enthused over the proposition to admit our wheat to the United States on terms dictated by Washington. I am in favour of free wheat and of free grain generally; I am in favour of the proposition as presented in 1911. If there was any classes of our community who were "in on velvet" in that proposition, they were the Canadian farmers and the Canadian millers. But the present Order in Council is altogether different. Let me call to the attention of the House the views of the Finance Minister as expressed in the debate to which I have referred and reported in Haneard of 1916, at page 870:
Then we have had petitions from mixed farmers. The mixed farmers say that bran and offal are more expensive in the United States than here and that consequently, if this went into effect, both in the Northwest and Ontario the farmer would have to pay more for his bran and offal. It is put forward also that if we took the step contemplated by this resolution the milling industry would certainly not be extended into the Northwest.
I have given that matter as careful consideration as I think I ever gave a question in my life, and I have come to the conclusion that if this were done the Canadian milling industry would not be extended further into the Northwest for this reason, that the markets lie to the east and south and while the milling would be done in Canada east of Winnipeg, to the extent that our millers might be able to carry it on with American competition, there is no likelihood, so far as we can judge at present, of an extension to the Canadian Northwest of the milling industry. I need not tell hon. members that upon the milling industry mixed farming largely depends for its well being. The offal, the bran which the farmers use for the rearing

of their livestock, is of supreme importance to the farming community and this proposed change would have an important bearing upon the supply of hran and offal for the rearing of stock by those engaged in the mixed farming industry. I think the small miller would probably disappear and that the business of the large millers would be very seriously affected if not crippled, and that the extension of the milling industry in the Northwest would be prevented.
I think the Minister of Finance was on solid ground in 1916 when he advanced that argument. I may frankly say that the Canadian millers opposed the proposition of 1911. It was opposed by the Minister of Finance. We heard in this House arguments why, if Canada wanted to negotiate with Washington, we should not have sent down two old men, but these two old men made a better bargain for Canada than that which is presented in the recently passed Order in Council that has at last been put through after six years of apprenticeship. Every carload of flour that comes into this country from the United States bagged in cotton sacks brings in free of duty 875 yards of cotton, and the Government, in admitting this cotton free into Canada, admits the products of United States cotton bag manufacturers. If the Canadian miller who is employing Canadian labour wishes to import these bags, he is met at the customs house with a tax. of 274 per cent.
Plus 74 per cent.

No, 20 per cent and 74 per cent. I have a quotation on bags from the Bemis Bag Company, manufacturing in St. Louis, Minneapolis, Kansas City and Winnipeg, and I find that the cost of bags is 84 cents a barrel cheaper in the United States than in Canada. That means that on his flour bags the Canadian miller is discriminated against to the extent of $19.04 per car, and notwithstanding what my hon. friends say about the monopolistic millers, I wish to say that there have been millions of bags of flour sold in this country to Britain and her Allies during the last two years upon which the millers got little more than $20 a carload profit. That may be a surprising statement, but I know that flour has been sold at practically the commission going to the Allies of Great Britain on the other side, and it may be said that $20 is not very much on a carload of flour.
Let me point out to the Minister of Finance how it works with regard to bran and shorts. The Canadian miller is enabled by the tariff to put bran and shorts upon the markets of the United States, but when the Canadian farmer wishes to buy bran and
shorts milled from Canadian wheat in United States mills, he is met at the customs house with a tariff of 25 per cent. Now, let us see how that works out. Bran at $30 a ton, with the duty of $7.50 per toil added, would cost $150 per carload duty. Canada, through its Government, says to the eastern farmer: for every car of bran you bring in here from the United States you must give us one of your best cows, and only when you have done so can you unload your car of bran. How can we expect the eastern farmer to increase the production of butter and cheese when he is met with such a tax upon the feed he requires for his animals? The Government recognize that bran and shorts are very important to the farming industry. I imagine that every hon. member in this House recently received from the Department of Agriculture special circulars Nos.
7 and 8 in which the department 4 p.m. urged the farmers to feed more bran and shorts to their live stock. The Department of Agriculture is urging the farmers to feed bran and shorts and the Department of Finance is placing an additional tax on bran and shorts coming into Canada.
How does the price of bran and shorts in Canada compare with the price on the .other side of the' line?

The price of bran at Buffalo on.the 29th May, as quoted, was $32.50 and on the same day it was quoted at from $36 to $38 in Toronto. The price in Boston was $34.50 and the same quotation would apply to Montreal as to Toronto. The shorts are a little higher, the spread b^ing greater in Canada than in the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What about the freight?

As I understand, Boston freight points are $2 a ton over Buffalo and Buffalo freight points are just about the same as Toronto freight points. I know that upon wheat the freight rates to Port Colborne and Buffalo are exactly the same and I imagine the same applies to bran and shorts. Under the present tariff arrangements' we are practically subsidizing the Canadian miller to export his product. He can buy bags cheaper in the United States, bring these bags into Canada, fill them with Canadian bran and shorts and export them and the Government gives him a rebate of 99 per cent of duty paid. I find here a quotation on bags for a carload of bran at $49.60. The duty is $13.40 and the refund,

if the bran and shorts are shipped out of the country, is $12.25; in other words, we have now a policy in Canada whereby we are subsidizing the Canadian miller to the extent of 60 cents a ton to put his bran and shorts out of the country. That is not an unfair way of presenting it because that is exactly the way it works out. Bran costing $30 a ton, when it is imported from the United States, pays a duty of $7.50 a ton. The Canadian miller can get his bran into the United States free. There is nothing to hinder him from putting out bran enough to create a scarcity in this country and to hold up the price to the Canadian feeder to the extent of $6 a ton over what it is in the United States. On this ground I would plead with the Minister of Finance to carefully reconsider the matter and put bran and shorts on the free list. If the Canadian miller is to maintain his output on the basis of last year, the minister must make some tariff changes. He must put cotton, jute and paper bags and flour milling machinery on the free list or what he predicted in 1916 will come true sooner than he thinks.
Who is going to build a mill anywhere in Canada when he can 'buy bags to sack his flour cheaper in the United States? Who will build a mill in Canada anyway when he can build it much cheaper in the United States? So I say to the Minister of Finance that if the farmers of eastern Canada are to have a .plentiful supply of bran and shorts for their cattle, and if the Canadian milling business is to continue to prosper, there must be some tariff changes.
Has my hon. friend the figures showing the shipments of bran and shorts both ways between the United States and Canada?
No.

I do not think it should require any argument to show the Minister of Finance that what my hob. friend (Mr. Robb) has just said is absolutely correct. It is absolutely unfair in the first place to make the miller pay a duty on his containers as against the American miller, who is not paying any duty on his containers. Bags can be purchased cheaper in the United States than here, and the Canadian miller has to pay a duty on them coming into Canada. The figures given by the hon. member for Huntingdon are not at all exaggerated. It is also unfair to ask us in Ontario, where more animal foodstuffs are fed than in any other part of Canada, to pay a duty on bran and shorts.

We want to have an open market for bran and shorts necessarily, and to get the feed as cheaply as we can. Before the removal of the duty on flour, etc., that did not make so much difference, but now that the duty has been removed, I am quite sure it does not require an argument to show the Minister of Finance, with his ability, that we should have free of duty the articles that my hon. friend has mentioned this afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Huntingdon (Mr Robb) has managed, in the course of his remarks, to speak to the amendment which was ruled out of order, -as well as to the amendment which is in order. 1 hope that I may be pardoned, therefore, if I reply very briefly to it- briefly because he has intimated that he may raise the question upon another occasion. He has referred to my remarks upon the subject of free wheat in 1916. The remarks which I made then, were, I believe, sound, having regard to the conditions which existed at that time:	It is
not my intention to go over the arguments which I put forward during the present session in support of the action taken by the Government in putting wheat upon the free list. It will be sufficient to say that the conditions now are' fundamentally different from the conditions which prevailed in 1916 when I made the Budget speech referred to. We on this side of the House are just as much interested as my hon. friend from Huntingdon or the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Nesbitt) in the live stock industry, and we nave shown it during our tenure of office by measures brought down for its development and increase. This Government may be depended upon to take such action at any time as may be necessary if the live stock industry of this country is in any way threatened with injury. I desire to say this: that bran and shorts have been and are to-day cheaper in Canada than in the United States, The hon. member for Huntingdon on the former occasion when he introduced this matter to the House during this session admitted it; he admitted that the prices in the United States were higher than in Canada. If that is so, it would not appear to me that there need be much apprehension on the part of the live stock industry in Canada that bran and shorts are going to flow from the United States into Canada.

The Finance Minister is quite correct; I did say that bran and shorts

were cheaper here than in the United States. But that was before the passage of this Order in Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend stated the matter fairly, and that was so, and it is so to-day. There may be local points at which bran or shorts are cheaper in the United States, although I do not know of any, but it must be borne in mind that freights play an important part in this matter. Take, for example, the district about Montreal served from the mills of Montreal. What about the freight rates? Any Canadian miller who desired to supply the United 'States market would have to pay freight rates on his ibran and shorts going out of this country to the United States. I am informed that there are no traffic rates governing bran and shorts from Montreal. Consequently, so far as the Canadian farmer in that district in which my hon. friend is particularly interested is concerned, there would seem to be no reason why bran and shorts should be dearer than across the line, and I am satisfied that the contrary is the fact. I have here a statistical statement published under the authority of the Secretary of Agriculture in the United States showing that for the years 1915, 1916 and 1917, the price as a whole of bran in the United States, per ton was, in 1915, $28.96; in 1916, $26.05, and in 1917, $38.33. For the State of Maine, the prices were: in 1915, $31.70; in- 1916, $29.70 and in 1917, $41.80. Whereas in Canada the price of bran at Toronto was on March 15( 1915, $28, which was lower than in the State of Maine and lower than the average price in the whole United States; it was $24 in 1916, which was lower than the price in the State of Maine and average price in the United States as a whole; and it was $37 in 1917, which was $1.33 lower than the average price in the United States; $4.80 lower than the price in the State of Maine; $3.60 lower than the price in New Hampshire, and $5.80 lower than in Massachusetts. The same is true with regard to other States, New York, Michigan and Minnesota, for which I have the prices here.
What was the price in Canada in 1917?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The wholesale price was $37.
We never bought any in 1917 at that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was at Toronto.
We never bought any at that price.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is not a good buyer.
I cannot help that. I tell my hon. friend that we are good buyers in our section of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What an unfair position hon. gentlemen take upon this question. They say: We are in favour of free wheat, and we were in favour of it in 1915. But now that it has been adopted they say: By reason of your putting wheat upon the free list, bran and shorts go out of the country and the result is that the price will be higher to the Canadian farmer. Is that a consistent position for hon. gentlemen to take? The inference is that wheat should not have been put on the free list. As I said, if any situation should arise by which the livestock industry might be injured by reason of there being a duty on bran and shorts, this Government may be depended on to meet it as it would any other difficulty. The figures which I have put forward are correct, and the situation at present is a sound situation so far as the price of bran and shorts in Canada and the United States is concerned. My hon. friend stated the other day that he was a miller, but so great was his love for the farmers of his district that, notwithstanding it would be a very serious thing to him as a miller, he wanted the duty taken off bran and shorts. That day he was speaking for the farmers; to-day he comes forward as a friend of the millers, and he is sitting cheek by jowl-with the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte), the avowed enemy of the millers in this House. Hardly a day passes that the hon. member for Richmond does not tell us of the tremendous profits made by millers, and he puts questions on the order paper asking the amount of excess profits we have taken from the miller. Yesterday I was able to show him that in the year 1915 we took from one milling company alone not less than $380,000. The member for Huntingdon says that the unfortunate miller will be ruined if the duty on cotton and jute bags and paper sacks is not removed. The whole discussion on free wheat which has agitated the House and the country for years past is now reduced to the monstrous injustice of the duty of 274 per cent on cotton and jute bags and paper sacks. That is what we have come down to in the Budget debate. Let us discuss the matter on its merits.

My hon. friend says: why should the miller have to pay duty on cotton and jute bags and paper sacks? He says that the Canadian millers are in competition with the millers of the United States. So they are as to flour, which comes in free of duty. But flour, cotton and jute bags and paper sacks are not the only commodities that come in. The milling industry is concerned in the manufacture of other things besides flour. My hon. friend has paid no attention to the other commodities on which the millers of Canada have a substantial protection. What are they? Buckwheat flour, general tariff, one-half cent per pound and 7i per cent war tax; corn flour, 25 per cent; rye flour, one-half cent per pound and 71 per cent war tax; oatmeal, three-fifths of a cent per pound and 7i per cent war tax; rolled oats, three-fifths of a cent per pound and 71 per cent war tax; wheat germ meal, 25 per cent; bran, 25 per cent; feed. 25 per cent-and only wheat flour and semolina on the free list. The principle involved in the tariff is this: if there is a protection of 25 per cent, as there is in some of these cases, that duty has been determined upon with due regard among other things, to the duties that the manufacturer has to pay upon his material coming in. My hon. friend admits that the millers, of which he is one, are protected to the extent that I have stated. I submit that nothing has especially been -brought to our attention which would warrant the Government in removing the duty from cotton and jute bags and paper sacks. This matter is of as little importance as any matter ever raised in a Budget debate. To show the House of how little importance it is, I point out that no miller in Canada, so far as I know, except the member for Huntingdon, has asked for the removal of the duty upon bags. My hon. friend says that the Canadian millers are in competition with the American millers, In the first place, they have the freights in their favour, I am informed that the cost of a 25 pound paper sack is 2 cents, of a 50 pound sack, about 4 cents, and of a cotton bag about 10 cents. In view of the protective duties which the millers enjoy upon their products other than flour, they have not asked us to take any action with regard to the duty upon bags. But the member -for Huntingdon is so -convinced that a grave injustice is being done the millers that he brings forward this resolution. If -at a time of a revision of the tariff, good -reason was shown for the reduction of these duties,' the Government would consider the 
situation. But this is not the time to- consider it, nor has the Government been asked to consider it by any one except the member for Huntingdon. My hon. friend's motion, therefore, is very trifling and unimportant indeed. If the matter were of consequence, the millers iwo-uld have brought it to the attention of the Finance Department.
I wish to call attention to another aspect of the case to which the member for Huntingdon has not adverted. Many industries in Canada are engaged in the manufacture of cotton and jute bags and paper sacks; they may be found in Winnipeg, Montreal, Toronto and other parts of Canada. These manufacturers have to pay duty upon the material which they import into Canada and upon all their machinery. Having regard to that fact, I think it would be -most improper to remove the duties from their product. If, as I say, upon a general revision of the tariff and in the light of the circumstances then prevailing, it would be advisable for the Government to give consideration to the question of the duty upon these hags and -sacks, the Government would do it, but in a proper way. It would have regard not only to the millers, hut to the manufacturers of bags, some of whom are engaged in large industries. Consideration would be given also to the material which they import and to the conditions of their industry. That principle underlies the whole tariff and all the duties imposed by it.
I have shown that so far as bran and shorts are concerned, the Canadian farmer is not likely under present conditions to suffer from our action respecting free wheat. I have stated that if he does suffer, this Government can be depended upon to deal with the situation as its. merits may warrant. I have shown also that the millers -I do not know that my hon. friend, although he is one of them, is authorized to speak for them all

have not deemed this matter of sufficient importance to bring it to 'the attention of the Finance Department. I have shown that they are protected under the tariff in respect of a great variety of their products. I have shown that the manufacturers of bags and paper sacks are interested in the duty upon these articles and that the matter should he dealt with, if it were advisable or necessary to deal with it, only upon a revision of the tariff. The amendment of the hon. member for Huntingdon should without hesitation be voted down, because it proceeds without

regard to the duty upon the products of millers other than flour and without any regard to the industrial' interests of those engaged in the manufacture of paper bags. Moreover, I know of no industry in Canada that is enjoying a greater prosperity during the war than the milling industry.
My hon. friend asserts that the milling industry will be seriously injured if the Government does not take the duty off cotton and jute bags anld paper sacks. It will be very interesting to see how the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) votes on this question. I would like to know what he has to say as to this. He says that the millers are making such tremendous profits that the Government should take possession of the mills, and .his desk-mate (Mr. Robb) says that the milling industry is suffering to such an extent that if we do not take the duty off bags, irreparable damage is going to accrue to that industry. It will be difficult for the hon. member for Huntingdon and the hon. member for Richmond to reconcile their views on the matter. The same remark applies to other hon. gentlemen who have spoken, not as the champions of the millers, but as their enemies. Some hon. gentlemen opposite have declared that this Government has been in a conspiracy with the western millers to prevent the farmers from getting a proper price for their wheat. The hon. member for Huntingdon now asks hon. gentlemen opposite to vote in favour of taking the duty off bags, a duty which is a source of revenue to this country in a time of war, arid the reason he gives is that the milling industry is suffering. When we come to vote on this matter, we shall see how hon. gentlemen opposite are going' to reconcile these two points of view, which, it seems to me, are almost irreconcilable.
I have dealt with the domestic business, and I have pointed out that the Canadian miller has the advantage of the local market which is always the best market. So far as concerns the export business, if the Canadian miller pays a duty on bags and fills those bags with Canadian flour and exports them to the United States or any other country, then, as my hon. friend from Richmond has stated, that miller receives a drawback of 99 per cent of the duty paid on those bags. Therefore, as regards the export business, he is on a par with other manufacturers of flour outside of Canada. It would seem to me that the hon. member is attaching an entirely disproportionate amount of importance to this
matter, and with all due respect I think he should not have taken the important step, although it is quite within his right, of moving what is really a vote of want of confidence in this Government, in respect of duties in regard to which, up to this date, no complaint has been made by any miller in Canada except himself.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has not dealt with this matter in the same spirit in which my hon. friend from Huntingdon introduced it, nor has he understood the spirit in which my hon. friend brought it before the House. It was the intention of my hon. friend to bring this question) up directly as a question of the free entry into Canada of 'bran and shorts, and on account of difficulties which arose under the rules of this House in regard to bringing up that motion, the amendment was launched in its present form, practically in order to get over a technicality. I think my hon; friend understood that. If he did not, in my judgment, he should have.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Will my hon.
friend allow me to state this? So far as I know there are two amendments before the House, one unconnected with the other, one ruled out of order, the other Tuled to be in order. The latter is the one that we are discussing.

That is the one I purpose discussing. What I say is that the hon. member for Huntingdon, at the beginning of his remarks, made it clear to any one who desired to understand him, that he was bringing this matter before the House, not in the interest of the millers, [DOT]but in the interest of the farming and dairying community in the county of Huntingdon. Had the hon. member been pleading his own case, I do not know that I would be willing to justify it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Will my hon.
friend be good enough to read the amendment?

I heard the speech of
the hon. member.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The amendment is based, on unfair discrimination against the millers.

I heard the amendment read, and I heard the speech of my hon. friend from Huntingdon, and I think the Minister of Finance understood it, and if he did not do so, it is because he did not

pay any attention to it. The hon. member's speech was base entirely upon the fact that under the present tariff items there,was an unjust discrimination against the farmers cf Ontario, and no special plea was made in favour of the millers. Had the previous ' amendment not been ruled out of order, the present amendment would not have been moved. The Minister of Finance says there is no demand for any change in regard to these items. I will grant that there is no demand from the millers, but surely imy hon. friend will not say he has no demand from the farmers of Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Well, the members in this House who represent the farmers of Ontario have certainly made strenuous demands upon the Minister of Finance, and have brought the matter to his attention as forcibly as we have been able to do so, and still the minister sits in 'his seat and does not intimate that there will be any relief. With all due respect to my hon. friend and to his great ability as a financier, I have this to say: that he has made a mistake in not making wheat products free as well as wheat. That is his mistake and he can rectify it without a general revision of the tariff. I will agree with him that this is no time for a general revision of the tariff, but he can rectify this slight mistake in regard to making wheat products free, just as last session he rectified what he considered an error in regard to apples. This is the situation in a nutshell. I cannot accept the Minister of Finance's statement in regard to prices. What he has given ns is the average price for the year, and he has quoted the average prices in 1915, 1916 and 1917 up to the present date. The minister does not buy on average prices; the farmers pf Ontario get the daily paper; they have the telephone, and when the opportunity comes to buy they do so, and they buy not on average prices, but the day's price.
I believe the figures which I submitted to the House a day or two ago, and which I will repeat to the House now, are absolutely correct. I was spoken to on Saturday last by farmers on the question of bran and shorts for feed; I made the inquiry, and I know that the prices which I am going to give are correct. The prices on Saturday last, as between Toronto and Buffalo, were as follows:-
Buffalo. Toronto.
Bran	532.50	538.00
Shorts or middlings.... 36.75	44.00 to $50.00
Those were the figures on the 29th of this month. I take the Montreal Gazette for

to-day, and I will give to-day's figures for Toronto: Toronto, mill feed prices, bran, $37 per ton; shorts, $43 per ton. I cannot give the Buffalo figures for to-day. The Toronto figures are per ton on track, Montreal freights, which applies to all points between North Bay and Toronto. There is, therefore, four or five dollars a ton difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is the differ ence along the boundary line east of Toronto? This tariff applies to the whole of Canada.
I do not understand the minister's question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has quoted prices at "Buffalo and Toronto. Those are only two points. What about Montreal and places in the adjoining states?

I will give the prices at Boston and Montreal.
Sir'THOMAS WHITE: And the freight rates.

Yes. At Boston on the 29th day of May bran was quoted at $34.50 per ton or $2 more than the price at Buffalo. Middlings were quoted at $38.75 per ton or $2 more than the price at Buffalo. On the same day the Montreal prices were bran, $38; shorts, or middlings, $44, with a spread up to $50. The freight rates are those which pertain to all points between North Bay and Toronto. I am not, however, going on the day's prices or on the prices given in the brokers' sheets. Men have come to me as recently as four or five days ago and have said: You are going to Ottawa, try, if possible, to get bran and shorts put on the free list. They know the situation and it has been brought to my hon. friend's attention by many hon. members on this side of the House so forcibly that he must have some reason for refusing to grant our request. Surely he can see that by making bran and shorts free, he is not going to injure anybody and he is going to help a very large number of people throughout the Dominion. Then why not take that course? See what an anomalous situation he has placed us in. We allow the wheat to go into the United States free, and yet we cannot get the bran from that wheat back into this country without paying a duty of 25 per cent. Our own wheat and our own bran go to the United States free, but we cannot get our own bran and ou>-own shorts and middlings back free.

Is it not a fact that
tremendous quantities of soft wheat come back to the Canadian miller from the Toledo district in Ohio, bringing the bran with it, under the free wheat regulation?

But there is not enough of it coming back, and the price shows that if the duty were removed $4 or $5 a ton would be the advantage the Canadian farmer would derive from it. As the hon. member for Huntingdon has pointed out, by reason of the drawback allowed on bags, there is a bonus of 60 cents a ton to the Canadian miller who exports his bran and shorts to the United States instead of selling them in Canada. This is a wrong that should be righted, and the Finance Minister with an assistant could right it in half an hour. We are not asking him to revise the tariff. We are simply pleading for a chance for the Canadian farmer to get cheaper feed for his hogs and for his cattle. As a matter of revenue this item amounts to nothing. I do not know whether the millers have asked for this or not, but whether or not, the farmers should be granted this relief; it is not going to hurt the millers. The figures I have given today are correct, or they were on the 29th. My hon. friend from Huntingdon presented the case iA a very striking manner when he said that a man who imports a carload of feed has to pay in duty the price of the best cow in his herd. Under the strained conditions that exist to-day, $150 is a pretty heavy tax for a man to pay who is feeding dairy cattle to be used as food for ourselves and our Allies.
I know that this amendment is practically a motion of want of confidence, and perhaps it is not the most appropriate way of bringing the matter to the attention of the House, but if the Finance Minister will assure us that he will study this matter out and give the farmers this relief, not next year, but next month, or even this month, we shall all be satisfied on this side of the House, and it will be one step in the right direction,

I am prepared to give my hearty support to any movement which has a tendency to reduce the price of mill feed to our farmers. But the motion which is before the House is not calculated to do that. Notwithstanding what my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) has said, this motion is intended for the benefit of the millers of this country. It reads:
That inasmuch as cotton jute, or paper sacks, when containing flour, now enter Canada from the United States free of duty, and inasmuch as Canadian millers-
Canadian millers, you will observe, not Canadian farmers.
-inasmuch as Canadian millers employing Canadian labour are handicapped because they are compelled to pay on empty sacks and bags, a duty of 27 J per cent on cotton and jute bags and sacks, and a duty of 35 per cent on paper sacks, this House is of the opinion that such unfair discrimination should be removed: Therefore it is resolved that in the opinion of this House, cotton and jute bags and sacks and paper sacks, when imported by millers for use in their own mills, should be free of duty.
The farmer or agriculturalist is not mentioned from beginning to end of that amendment, nor is there any reference to him either direct or indirect, nor to the consumer either. It deals with the millers entirely, and in my humble judgment the millers in this country are not suffering, and are not entitled to any special consideration from this House. When the hon. member for Huntingdon was on his feet, I asked him for the import and export figures as between Canada and the United States for bran and mill feed, but he did not have them. I have now before me the figures for the years 1915 and 1916, which show that our imports from the United States of bran, mill feed, etc., amounted to $47,778 in 1915, and to $43,700 in 1916. Our exports of bran to the United States amounted to $778,626 in 1915, and to $1,602,158 in 1916. The Finance Minister this afternoon has given us the price of bran and mill feed in Canada and the United States for the past three years, and the figures indicate that the prices in Canada for the last three years have been uniformly lower than on the other side of the line. I think my hon. friend from Huntingdon admitted that. The hon. member for South Wellington has also given us the figures for one or two days at one or two points in the United States and Canada.
Those were governing points, both for Canada and the United States.

We have the figures
of the hon. member for one or two days at what he says were governing points in this country and the United States. In addition to that, and the statement of the Minister of Finance, we have our import and export figures for bran and mill feed, as between this country and the United States. If the hon. member for South Wellington is Tight in his statement that bran and shorts are

cheaper on the other side of the line, then why in the name of heaven do the people of the United States, who are always supposed to have a pretty strong grip on the dollar, come over here and pay a higher price for our bran? We cannot overlook our export and import figures, and they emphatically indicate that the price on the other side of the line is higher than the price in Canada.

Then why maintain the duty?
Mr. EDW1ARDS: I have given these figures in controversion of what my hon. friend has said, and they indicate that the statement of the Minister of Finance is to be taken in preference to the statement of the hon. member from South Wellington.
Then why maintain the duty?	'

Let me give the hon.
member a reason why we should not interfere with the duty-a reason which he applauded until he almost raised blisters on his hands when the matter came up in the session of 1912-1913. Let me quote the words of his own leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, uttered in the House on that occasion (Hansard p. 30):
Once a duty is imposed that duty should not lightly be interfered with.
He was referring to the duty on cement. The hon. member for South Wellington supported that; he said that it was perfectly right. The motion arose out of the Government's determination to cut the duty on cement in two. When hon. gentlemen opposite were in power, they did not show the farmers of this country much consideration in the matter of cement, which is used by our farmers all over the country, for they immediately raised the duty on cement coming from the United States. They immediately increased the duty on 'cement coming into this country from the United States. Under the National Policy of the Conservative party there had been a duty on cement, but bags containing the cement were free. But that did not suit hon. gentlemen opposite. Supported by the hon. member for South Wellington, they not only increased the duty on cement, but put a special duty on the bags containing cement. Why? Because they had such gentlemen as Senator Edwards and others in the cement merger, who are making hundreds of thousands of dollars out of the farmers by squeezing them on the price of

cement. In this and scores of other cases that I could mention, where their friends are affected, their views about customs duties do not amount to a snap of your finger. If their friends can reap the benefit ,and take money from the pockets of the people, they will arrange the duties accordingly.

Is the hon. member
(Mr. Edwards) in favour of removing or of maintaining the duty on bran and shorts?

The hon. member (Mr. Guthrie) need not smile as if he thought he had asked me something that I would not answer. Hon. gentlemen opposite, including the hon. gentleman from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) might smile when putting a question for information to hon. members on this side if we were like themselves and had as many policies as there are members. Every person knows that the Liberal party is a conglomerate, so far as their tariff policy is concerned of-
Not Nationalist and Tory.

Where did the Nationalists learn their lesson? Let me tell the hon. member for Edmonton there is not a treacherous Nationalist utterance by Bour-assa, Lavergne, or any other in the province of Quebec, but has its counterpart in the utterances of his own leader at different times in his career.
May I ask the hon. member to permit me to say that what he has stated is incorrect in substance and in fact?

I do not know that the fact that the hon. member for Edmonton says that my statement is incorrect will materially alter the opinions of the people of this country. My word in this House or out of it is as good as his, and my record is as good as his. Now, to revert to the question asked by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). Gould anything be plainer or fairer than the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), that as soon as this Government perceives that the farmers can be benefited by a change of duties in regard to bran and shorts he is ready and willing to give that change? And he states the reason why there is no necessity for that change now-that the prices of bran and shorts in the United States are higher today than the prices on this side of the line. That is perfectly satisfactory to me, and I think that in so stating I answer the hon. gentleman. I am in favour of removing the

duty on bran and shorts as soon as it can *be shown that 'by so doing we shall benefit the farmers of this country, but I am not in favour of it merely because some hon. gentleman gets up and produces figures, or makes statements, which, in my humble judgment, when coming from the other side of this House, may always be taken with a liberal supply of salt. The hon. member for South Wellington, speaking in this House no longer ago than the dajf before yesterday, said:-
I do not believe at any time in tho haphazard revision of the tariff. I think that such a revision should be gone about systematically and scientifically. I think the tariff should be revised from time to time, and I hope that when the revision does take place, after hostilities are closed, we will be able to revise it downward. But I think that of all times this is about the most inopportune to disturb the industries and business of this country.
I agree with him; in ifact, I might have quoted the words of the hon. member as an answer to the question that he asked me a moment ago; I went a little further in stating my opinion on this question of the duty on bran and shorts. But have these gentlemen any right to get up, and, under the cover of a motion intended for the benefit of the millers only, pose as the friends of the farmer? I say they have not. The whole course of the Liberal party in this country is one showing absolute disregard for the farmers except to try and hoodwink and blindfold them. Take their position in regard to farm implements, -for instance. We had the spectacle here the other day of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), and the hon. member for Moose-jaw (Mr. Knowles) advocating the removal of the duty on farm implements. Yet, a few years ago, when the proposition was made by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Sehaffner) to reduce the duty on these implements, the hon. member for Assiniboia, assuming to speak for western 'Canada, said that the motion of the hon. member for Souris ought not to be approved. And the hon. member for Moosejaw took the same position. But that is not all. These hon. gentlemen when ip office did make a change which was nominally a slight reduction of the duty on agricultural implements. The duty on binders at that time was 20 per cent, and they cut it down to 17} per cent. But at the same time they went to the manufacturers and said: You need not be a particle scared; we know what we are doing; we are simply doing this to satisfy the farmers, but we will fix it all right for
119	*
you. And so they did. When the duty was 20 per cent the valuation for duty of a binder was $80, so that the duty was $16. But when they reduced the duty to 17} per cent, they raised the valuation to $100, so that the duty collected was $17.50. That is the way they played the game of the manufacturers while pretending to the farmers that they were going to cut off the head of protection and trample on its body -that they were going to wade in gore, so far as protection was concerned. The whole object evidently was to hoodwink the farmers just the same as in the case of cement. They raved about the cement duty in their speeches in one part of the country, pretending that they would meet the wishes of the farmers. But they framed their tariff in such a way as to put hundreds of thousands of dollars into the pockets of Senator Edwards and other Grit,heelers-excuse me, I would rather say, partisans of their own-whom they wanted to please. As a friend near me suggests, that is the policy they have pursued for fifteen years, a policy which differs in every part of the country. There are 221 constituencies in this country, and for the Liberal party there are 221 different tariff policies. That party, so far as tariff matters are concerned, is a thing of shreds and patches.
Down in one part of the country they want free potatoes. The hon. member for Car-leton- (Mr. Carvell) is for free potatoes, ,or he would fix the price of potatoes but only after he had sold his. Pure jealousy! He would put the price of potatoes down to $1.75 a bag when he had not any more to sell because he did not want his neighbours to get $3 or $2.50 just as he wanted to fix the price of hay. Then these hon. gentlemen come and plead that they are the friends of the farmer. I represent an agricultural constituency. I am certainly satisfied, representing the farmers of my part of the country, with the stand that the Minister of Finance has taken on this matter and the assurance that he has given the House this afternoon. I am satisfied that he will deal with this matter in the interest of the farmers as well as all other classes of the community fairly and at the proper time.

speechtext: The point of order is well taken, but if latitude is allowed to one hon. member, another hon. member on the other side should not be unduly restricted in reply. I ask the hon. member-

speechtext:
I ask the hon. member not to pursue that subject because it may lead to acrimonious discussion, detrimental

to the orderly and proper consideration of the question before the House.
I am not in the least degree acrimonious nor do I feel out of temper in the slightest
What would you be if you tried to be acrimonious?

I did not quite hear the observation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. If it is for the winning of the war I would be pleased to listen but if not it does not matter, I suppose. I have not often the honour of being interrupted by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and I am sorry I did not hear what he said because I would like respectfully to reply to him. But what I was pointing- out-and I will be brief and cut it down-is that I am sick and tired of supporters of the Government, whenever they get on their feet, no matter what the subject is, turning to Nationalism and trying to represent that the origin and beginning and genesis of Nationalism is with the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). If Nationalism is bad, if Bou-rassaism is bad, if Lavergneism is bad, why did they take them to their hearts in 1911?
Order.
Why are they hugging Nationalism to their hearts to-day and glad to have it?
Order, order.
They live with it.
Order.

They live with it; they try to keep it up; they sleep with it; they tried to breed it in 1911 and they have tried to breed it again. Now, that is all I propose to say on that subject. I promise my hon. friends opposite that every time they bring up this subject we will have something to say about it.
The resolution now before the House is a sort of double barrelled arrangement. There is a resolution that is said to be out of order and another resolution that is in order, and we have been to some extent discussing the one that is out of order on the one that is in order. I am not breaking imy neck in trying to bring any great favours to the millers of this country unless they will show some fruit worthy of repentance and some fruit worthy of being cuddled and cared for by the Government of this
119*	\< f | |
country and by this Parliament. In the /part of the country from which I come, rwe had always hoped that when the West was developed, when we had given them plenty of railways, when we had plenty of wheat, we in the far East, who are practically non-producers of flour, would have cheap flour and cheaper living. In Nova Scotia we .produce large quantities of coal, iron, steel, fish, lumber and other materials, but we do not produce enough flour to feed our people. We therefore are very much interested in cheap flour. The Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance have done nothing to help out the situation in reference to the high cost of living and the cost of the product of the (miller. The Minister of Finance makes the proud boast that he took $238,000 from one milling concern in Ontario. That milling concern immediately started to tax the fisherman, the lumberman, the farmer of the province of Nova Scotia and of other provinces until it could get back three times the amount which the minister is so proud of having t'aken from it. The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Moffioy) the other day informed us that the flour which is to-day bought in Sydney and by the working classes of Glace Bay, Sydney Mines and North Sydney at $17 a barrel was ground of wheat that was bought at $1.70 a bushel.
Less than that.

And less than that,
f think that the people of this country [DOT]have a right to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce not to allow the millers to pile on this enormous profit. Why does he permit the millers to rob the people of Canada by selling flour at $17 a barrel that could have been sold at $8.50 or $9. I want to point out to the Minister of Finance that the money he takes from the millers and other big concerns is simply taxed back by them upon the poor men of this country, and that it is a fallacy to say that it is taken from the wealthy men. We had an illustration of the same thing in the United States a few years ago. When that great financier Rockefeller gavie $25,000,000 for the purposes of education to the federal treasury of the United States, he immediately turned around and added half a cent to the price of oil, and in less than a fortnight he had his $25,000,000 back. That is what is happening in the case of the millers, the money that he takes from them they tax back upon the poor people of this country. That is the explanation of flour selling at $17 a barrel to-day. If any favours are to be

granted to the millers we, the common people of this country who have to buy the .products of the millers, would like to see that we are getting some benefit from it. Something should be done by the Government for the relief of the poor man who is earning $2 or $2.50 a day, whc finds it almost impossible to pay #17 for flour, 50 or 52 cents a pound for butter, and 40 or 50 cents a pound for beef. He cannot pay that out of the miserable pittance he receives in wages. I asli the minister to come to the rescue of the poor people and relieve them from the horrible and unbearable burdens which they have to carry by reason of the high cost of living, the exorbitant prices of many of the things they consume.

Does the hon. member
think that free flour has effected any relief to the people of this country?

I am not talking about the tariff on flour. I say that the Government of this country, like those of other countries, should forbid the owner of flour, whether a miller or a middleman, from selling it at an exorbitant price. I know nothing to prevent the flour owners in the 'United States combining with the flour owners in this country and imposing a 'similar burden on the poor of the two nations. We are looking for some measure of real relief, not the haphazard measures that have been taken toy this Government.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
A reply is allowed to a member who has made a substantive motion before the House, but not to a member who has moved an amendment. It is understood that the hon. member for Huntingdon is to be allowed the privilege of a reply by the consent of the House and in accord with an arrangement previously come to.
Mr . J. A. ROBB (Huntingdon): The Finance Minister said that I had introduced a resolution to help the millers, and then went on to point out that I made a speech to help the farmers in connection with free bran and shorts. But later on both the Minister of Finance and the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) laid stress on the fact that all our efforts this afternoon were to advance the cause of the millers, notwithstanding that the Minister of Finance had said that our speeches were altogether in favour of free bran and shorts. I am very much encouraged with the statements of the Finance Minister and the member for Frontenac. The Minister of Finance has said that the farmers may trust this Government to do what is fair
XHr. McKenzie.]
and to put them in a right position, and the member for Frontenac has also said that just as soon as it can be proved conclusively that the farmers are wronged the Government will make it right. I want to explain the effect of .free wheat on these prices. The Order in Council was passed on the 16th April. On the 14th April bran was worth $43.50 a ton in Buffalo and $38 a ton in Montreal and Toronto. On the 28th April it was $43.25 in Buffalo and $43 in Montreal. There was no advance in the United States, rather a reduction, but an advance of $5 a ton in Canada. That is what I complain of exactly. The Minister of Finance has given quotations for 1915, 1916 and 1917. He is living in the dead past. He gave quotations on bran and shorts under conditions that existed before they passed this Order in Council. But as soon as the Minister of Finance passed his Order in Council, which permitted bran and shorts t6 go free into the United States, but put a tax of 25 per cent upon them coming into Canada he reversed those conditions. The minister will find that in one or two years from now the conditions will be altogether changed.
Does the hon. gentleman consider that the increase in the price of bran and shorts in Canada, to which he has been referring, is a hold-up by the millers?

I am inclined to think that the hon. gentleman has guessed correctly. The tariff compels the millers to pay 27i per cent duty on cotton and jute bags and 35 per cent on paper sacks. The Finance Minister has admitted that the figures which I gave were correct. He himself quoted figures in corroboration of what I said: that the cost of sacking flour in Canada was 8J cents a barrel greater than the cost of sacking in the United States.
The minister lays stress on the assertion-that I am the only miller who has complained. If he digs down deep enough into his own department he will find there a letter published in Canadian newspapers on Christmas Day, 1913, and signed, I think, by Mr. Black, of the Ogilvie Milling Company. Of that I am not sure; at any rate, it was signed by a large miller in Montreal, and it pointed out to the Government that if they passed an Order in Council accepting conditions imposed on Canada by Washington they would compel the millers to join those who were agitating for free admission of many articles into Canada, particularly of bags, sacks and milling machinery.

I was proceeding, when interrupted, to point out that conditions have changed ' since the Order in Council was passed. Bran and shorts to-day are worth $32.50 in the United States and $38 at points in Canada taking the same freights. These freights are what are known as zone freights. The price of bran or flour is fixed largely on the basis of blanket freights. In respect of goods going into the United States, Boston or Buffalo would be zone freight points.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Are there through freight rates on bran and shorts from Montreal to United States?
I should not think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If there are not through freight rates, then why should bran and shorts go from Montreal and surrounding districts into the United States? I am asking a question based on information which I obtained from one of the leading manufacturers of flour, bran and shorts in Canada, who told me that there were no through freight rates from the district in which Montreal is situated to the United States.

That is quite right. The basis of all these prices is the rate on products coming from the West. In the Northwest, where the big mills are-Winnipeg, Moosejaw, Kenora, Fort William-or at Port Colborne, there are no cattle to eat the feed, which must be shipped east. The price is based on its value delivered at blanket freights. The production of bran and shorts in Montreal is only a bagatelle compared with what is required in this country; even in eastern Canada the supply is not sufficient. My complaint is that the millers can create scarcity by taking advantage of these through freights and shipping to the New England market via Buffalo and Niagara Falls. They are encouraged to do this by the duty on hags, which gives them a rebate on all bags exported. I think, therefore, that 1 have proved to the minister that conditions have changed since the Order in Council was passed. I am encouraged to believe that he will change his mind and make some tariff changes.
I know that the resolution which I have presented is out of order, but it was brought in to enable the House to discuss the question. With the permission of the House, therefore, I withdraw the amendment.
