How many of these cruisers are on Atlantic coast?

Last year we chartered a boat to take the place of the Government cruiser Margaret, which we got two or three years ago, but which was sent to Halifax when war was declared. Last year we got a steamer, the Dollard, from the Marine and Fisheries Department, but this year we have been unable so far to arrange for a steamer, the Dollard having been sent to Halifax on naval service. The Government steamers are all in use. It has always been the custom to have an item of this kind for that service. We have another little steamer, the Alert, down at Sydney. I think that is the only steamer that comes out of that port.
Has the Government recently chartered a steamer for customs preventive service in the St. Lawrence?

Not that I know of. I do
not know of any being under order.

I am informed that Mr. W. M- Macdonald of Sydney recently purchased in the United States a steamer which he has chartered to the Department of. Customs and which is at present undergoing repairs on the marine slip at Point Tupper. Has the minister any information to give to the committee on that matter?

A charter would not be made until I had been consulted, and no charter or offer of that kind has as yet reached me. The chief officer of the Preventive Service, Mr. Wilson, who is in charge of such vessels, when we were informed by the Marine Department that we could not have the marine steamer, DollaTd, has been making inquiries for some little time, and he may possibly have been discussing this matter with the gentleman mentioned by the hon. member, but if he has, I have never heard of it before nor has the matter been submitted to me.

I was at Sydney a few days ago, and the statement was made that this

*steamer had been purchased for the purpose of chartering her to the Government for the customs service, and I want to know from the minister if any negotiations to that end have recently been on foot.

I do not think I can make the matter clearer than I have done. No negotiations have as yet been submitted to me, and I have not heard of any; but negotiations may be going on with the officials of the department, and when they come to some decision as to what they think would be fair to submit to me for my approval, I would it of it then. Therefore, I am not in a position to say that no negotiotions heve been going on. It may be possible that the officials have been carrying on negotiations, but nothing has yet *reached me.

Are these cruising
steamers in the preventive service supposed to see that American fishermen do not fish within the three mile limit? Has the Alert anything to do with that? I know, when the late Captain Borden was in the service of the Customs Department it was part of his duty at certain seasons of the year to ,see that American fishermen did not come within the three mile limit. While he was performing the same service that the Alert is performing now, he made several captures. The Alert is a very slow concern; she is supposed to overtake other vessels, and I suppose it is the intention that she will overtake them on the same principle that the lion catches the jackal; when the jackal makes a run all around the country, he gets confused and Tuns into the lion's mouth. If the Alert catches anything, it will certainly be on that principle, because I understand she is a very slow boat. It so happens, however, that while she is slow, she is owned by a very fast crowd, and that no doubt suits the ideas of the minister, and he will pass over all the sins of omission and commission of the Alert so long as the one great aim and purpose is served of putting money into the pockets of his Tory friends. 1 want to remind the minister that I hope this Alert will keep within her proper bounds. Of course, her speed is such that it is not difficult for her to keep within any bounds, hut this boat was not always in the preventive service. She was hired for preventive work, but she was willing to do other things in the interest of the Tory party. She used to be chartered by this

Government and by my bon. friend who presides over the department for carrying election rum down to different parts of Victoria county.
She was pretty fast then. I am surprised that the hon. member says she was a slow boat, because I thought at that time she was pretty swift.

She got her name into a code which was made by which the workings of the department in connection with the Alert was understood. It so happened that we discovered the code through the very name of the Alert. This code name was appearing so often in the code telegrams that at last we discovered that this boat was being referred to, and once we found out that this meant the Alert, of course, we unravelled the whole business, and I must admit that in that case she was swift-in bringing destruction to the Tory party, because once we found out what those telegrams meant the results weTe startling. What I want to impress upon the minister is this, that there will he elections again, and there will possibly be byelections, and I want, in all seriousness, to impress upon him that the money that comes into his hands and that he is expending in connection with the public service of this country is furnished by Grits and Tories alike, and I think that the minister will concede at once that it is most unfair to compel the Grits to supply the funds to carry on a Tory campaign, because, when we were furnishing the money to run the Alert and to pay her captain and crew, we were furnishing the money to fight against ourselves. I am sure the minister will rise to the lofty eminence of saying to the officers of the department that they must not prostitute the service and departmental property to such purposes as they used the Alert and everything belonging to it in those days. I am not speaking in a haphazard way, because all these facts were brought out in the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, and it was shown that all facilities of Government were put at the disposal of the Tory party in that connection. Not only the Alert, but the telegraph system and the telephone system of the Government were put at their disposal in the same way. I wish to give the minister notice that if he should again commit such a reckless error as that we shall not promise to deal with him in such a mild manner as I am doing in bringing this maJtter before him now. I hope hereafter that each party will pay their own

election expenses, and that Tories will not he permitted to put their hands into the public treasury and to take out Grit money for the purpose of-fighting the Grits.

I agree with the hon. member that Government steamers, or Government property, should not be used in such cases as the hon. member has stated. I do not think that is fair. I think the position taken by the hon. member is absolutely right. I remember the case that the hon. member mentions. I did not know, of course, at the time that a Government steamer had been used for any other purpose than that for which she was chartered.
Didn't you get a telegram?	-
No, not in any shape or form. ,1 did not know anything about it.

We were inquiring
in the House about it.

That was after the boat had started on the trip. As soon as the matter was brought to my attention, I had the boat stopped. They tell me-I don't know whether it is true or not-that Government steamers were used for this purpose when an election came on under the late Government.
Who told you that?
Not the hon. member. However, whether it was done ot not, I do not think it is right.
What does the Alert cost a month?
31,250. She is paid the same rate as the Gladiator, whose place she took.
Where is the Dollard stationed?

She runs anywhere on the
St. Lawrence, from Quebec down to Anticosti, the Magdalen Islands, and all around those waters. She has taken the place of the Margaret, and is in the same service. We have not been able to charter any steamer so far this season, but we shall be glad to get one if we can.

How many are on
-the staff at New Glasgow?
There are six: J. Fred McDonald, H. W. Baillie, H. D. Gillis, S. T. McCurdy, S. M. McKenzie, and A. A Clay.

Has Mr. Clay been
permanently appointed?

He has not been appointed
permanently up to the present. He was put on as a landing waiter on August 16, 1915.
He is not a returned soldier?
I could not say.

Is it intended to
make his appointment permanent?

Before taking a man on we
generally have him examined by the inspector or collector as to hie fitness for the position; if satisfactory, he is appointed on probation for six months, and if he makes good he is then appointed permanently. I know of no reason why Mr. Clay has not been permanently appointed, and now that my hon. friend has brought the matter to my attention, I will have an Order in Council passed appointing him if everything is satisfactory.
It has been stated that Mr. Macdonald is going to retire. Has the minister heard anything of that?
There has been no application from him for superannuation and retirement. He has been in the service since 1879. If he retires-, he would be entitled to 70 per cent of his salary, about $1,260.
If he retires, will a returned soldier be appointed in his place?

Yes, but we might have to fill the position temporarily until we can find a returned soldier qualified for the position. At the present time we have a number of returned soldiers acting as relieving officers, taking the place of those who are absent on holidays or from sickness. If Mr. McDonald retired, and I was not able to get a returned soldier in that constituency to fill the position, I would get one from outside.
There are plenty of returned soldiers there.
He would have to be qualified for the position.
Would he have to be recommended by the man in charge of the patronage?
We take the best man we can get
I am speaking of returned soldiers.

I have not heard of any
patronage committee in that riding. I am

the only patronage committee for the Customs Department.

As the hon. gentleman has never heard of a patronage committee in my constituency, I might remind him that he has never asked me to recommend any appointments, and perhaps I may he said to represent the people there. Where does my hon. friend get his information about there being no patronage committee in my constituency?
I make inquiries of my own. There is no patronage committee.
Only some particular gentleman who happens to have your confidence, I suppose?
I know a lot of people.

I am a little curious - about this. There was a vacancy in the postmastership at Stellarton a few weeks ago, but although the minister claims great credit for having always appointed returned soldiers, this position was given to a man who was not a returned soldier, but was recommended by the local chairman of the Conservative Committee. There were quite a few returned soldiers in the district who were quite competent to fill the position, which did not require any technical training. In view of the experience in my own constituency I do not know whether my hon. friend's protestations in regard to returned soldiers are to be regarded seriously. Perhaps a different policy is followed in the Post Office Department.

I am following the Order in Council and appointing returned soldiers wherever possible. I understand the same policy is followed by all the departments, but I have enough to do to look after my own department. I have already appointed over 233 returned soldiers, and there are still a number of good positions vacant. When a vacancy occurs the people, of course, are very anxious that a returned soldier in that constituency should receive the appointment. Men are coming back wounded in much greater numbers than before. I had a letter to-day from a man in an Ontario constituency telling me about a young man who had occupied a splendid position and who is now back from the war having suffered the loss of a leg, and asking me if I could give him a position. I was pleased to be able to say that I could, and in his own constituency. That is the policy I have pursued. If, for instance, a vacancy

should occur in the hon. member's constituency, and a soldier should return to that constituency who was qualified to fill the position, I should be glad to appoint him.
Is that the policy in the other departments of the Government?
I have told the committee about the Order in Council on the subject.

It does not seem /to be the policy of the Department of Public Works. In my constituency last September a returned soldier was appointed to the position of caretaker of a public building, a position not calling for very great skill or ability. The man got notice from Ottawa of his appointment. But there was an election, and a man there who was not a returned soldier, but who represented about a dozen votes, threatened to bolt the party unless he got the position, so they turned down the soldier and gave the place to the politician. I only wanted to know whether the hon. minister was speaking for himself or for the Government.

I know that the Order in Council was passed, and I do not know that the other departments are acting differently from my own. At the same time, I am looking after my own department, and I suppose each head of a department will be able to speak for himself.
Would the minister regard with any degree of interest or attention a letter that I might write to him with regard to a returned soldier?
If there is a position vacant and a returned soldier fit to fill the position I will appoint him.
Would the minister ask the attention of the Post Office Department to a case that I might lay before him?
I am pretty busy attending to my own department.

When another minister goes away, it seems quite the custom to call the hon. gentleman (Mr. Reid) to take temporary charge of the department. I think he has acted for almost every one of his colleagues except the Prime Minister. I am bound to say that he is one of the most competent men in the Government, and it is on that account that I appeal to him, because I feel that he could exercise a good influence upon his colleague, whoever he may be, who is Acting Postmaster General. A vacancy occurred in my con-

stituency in April last, but there was not the slightest suggestion of appointing a returned soldier, though there are quite a number of returned soldiers any one of whom would be competent to fill the position. Will not the minister be good enough to call the attention of the Post Office Department to this matter? Who is Acting Postmaster General?
Mr. Patenaude.

Will not the Minister of Customs call the attention of the Acting Postmaster General to the fact that the provisions of the Order in Council which has been referred to have not been observed with Tegard to the appointment of a postmaster in the town of Stellarton, in my constituency. The hon. gentleman is in more direct communication with the Acting Postmaster General than I am.

I had to go to the Acting Postmaster General a few months ago with regard to a vacancy in my own constituency. We had a vacant post office there-quite a nice position. I asked the Acting Postmaster General to fill it temporarily until we could find a returned soldier who could fill it suitably. Of course, the hon. gentleman said that that was the intention. That position in my constituency is held until there is a returned soldier to fill it.
Who was appointed temporarily?

A girl who has been in the department ten or twelve years fills it temporarily, with some assistance. The other day, the case was mentioned of the postmastership of Smiths Falls, in the constituency adjoining mine. The question was asked whether it was the intention to appoint a returned soldier, and the Acting Postmaster General replied that it was. I will mention the case of Stellarton, and will say that I hope that the same policy that I am following is being carried out in other departments.
Has the minister reached a - conclusion with regard to the customs col-lectorship at Montreal?
That was fully discussed last night, as the hon. member will see by referring to Hansard.

There was an officer of the Customs Department in North Sydney, a Mr. Brennan, who went to the front as an aviator. He returned wounded, but, having recovered, has gone back to the front again.
His position in the customs service has been filled, but not by a returned soldier. Can the minister tell me whether this appointment to succeed Mr. Brennan is only temporary, or whether the new man has been permanently appointed?

Mr. Brennan, as the hon. gentleman has stated, is absent on active service. When a vacancy occurs in this way, -the policy is, as I have stated, to put in a relieving officer, on the understanding that he holds the position only until the soldier returns, or until it is ascertained that he will not be able to return. That was the policy previous to the Order in Council. This may be the man who was appointed- Hector W. McNeill.

That is the man who
was appointed.

He is on the list as an acting officer. If he had been appointed prior to the Order in Council, and if he has been acting since, I would not feel justified in dismissing him now until we see what is the result in so far as Mr. Brennan is concerned.

I understand it is the
policy in regard to the inside service that, if a man enlists, his salary goes on irrespective of whatever pay he gets as a soldier. Does that rule apply to the outside service as well? I am not begrudging Mr. Brennan anything he may be getting. I am asking if this young gentleman, who left his position in the customs at North ;Sydney and who is performing service at the front as an aviator, comes within that rule or gets the salary that he was getting from the department before he enlisted?

The rule is the same for
both services. The Order in Council passed first gave the full salary. Then, in 1915 it was provided that they would get the one salary. The Orders in. Council apply to both the inside and outside services. As far as Mr. Brennan is concerned, he would come under the first Order in Council were it not, as I have been informed, that he enlisted in the Imperial flying corps, and not in the Canadian Overseas Forces. If Mr. Brennan had enlisted in the Canadian Overseas Forces prior to November 1, 1915, he would come within this rule of getting his full salary. But, if after that he would simply -get the difference between his military pay and his civil service pay.

I do not know the date of Mr. Brennan's enlistment but I know

he took a course in aviation and enlisted in Canada. Evidently he put himself at the disposal of the powers that be and when he got across I do not know where they put him. We had no Canadian aviation corps at the time and I suppose he was (willing to go wherever they put him. He certainly enlisted, received his commission and took his course in Canada before He went across'.
IMr. REID: I remember that the Imperial Government had an aviation -school and were enlisting for their own Imperial forces. Any official who enlisted in the aviation corps received a commission from the Imperial Government and not from the Canadian Government and, of course, he would not come within the Order in Council. Therefore, Mr. Brennan is not getting anything from the Customs Department but he would probably be getting more in the aviation corps than the amount of his salary here. I do not think there will be very much difference.

I would like the minister to look into it. If Mr. Brennan, as a member of the outside service of the department, would be entitled to a continuation of his salary if he had enlisted in the Canadian service, he should not be deprived of that advantage because of the particularly useful and hazardous course he had to take or because he had to go into the Imperial Service, particularly in view of the fact that we had no aviation corps of our own that he could have joined.

This is the first time this
matter had been brought to my attention. Cases of this kind would be very few, as faT as I can see, and I think they might be -very generously dealt with. But, they would not come within the scope of the Order in Council as it now is. I will take that matter up. It is one that can he settled at any time by ah application from Mr. Brennan or any one else that has enlisted in that way. It might open up a question though in quite a lot of cases because there are a large number of men from *Canada who have gone over and enlisted in the same way.

Mr. Brennan belongs
to my town but he is not a supporter of *mine at all. I wish the minister would remember what I am saying and that he would give me an assurance, that if an application is made on behalf of this gentleman, it will be considered.

Indians, Ontario and Quebec-Relief, medical attendance and medicines, $28,000.

On this item I wish to express my gratitude to the hon. gentleman for what he has done towards maintaining a hospital for the Indians at Caughnawaga. For many years it was known that the Indians were exposed, especially to tuberculosis, until a certain lady from France devoted her fortune to help those poor unfortunates. Although she had quite a large fortune, yet the maintenance of a hospital at Caughnawaga required the help of the Government. I appealed not in vain to the present Minister of the Interior, and he very graciously acquiesced to the request to aid that hospital. I am proud to say that with what has been given annually for the maintenance of that hospital the lady in question has been in a position to grant a very considerable relief to the band at Caughnawaga. Now that my hon. friend has done so nobly for that cause, I would appeal to him again, this time not for financial aid, because I understand that for the present he has done well enough towards the institution. But for the last two years a quarry which, I think, belongs to the Government as it is on the reserve, has been exploited by a gentleman in Montreal, Mr. Giroux, in virtue of a contract passed with one of the departments. That quarry is in the neighbourhood of the institution and as a result of its exploitation there is, first, the noise which is very annoying to the patients, and, secondly, a dust which invades the institution much to the worry of the medical staff, the nurses and the inmates. May I press the minister to see that this quarry is not further exploited. I believe that stone can be extracted from another point on the reserve, and surely the welfare of the sick and the staff of the hospital should take precedence over the little profits which might be made from the operation of the quarry. I think the minister might safely put the matter into the hands of his deputy by whom it would be dealt with expeditiously. In fact, I have taken on myself to interview Mr. Scott on two occasions, and we have appointed ourselves a delegation to wait on the minister in order to see if this annoyance cannot be abated.

I understand there have been some negotiations between the com-

pany having the lease for the stone quarry and the department, and that some complaints have been made to the department regarding the noise, dust, etc. The company has promised to mitigate these annoyances to the greatest possible extent, although I do not know if the noise can be abated. If stone could be removed from another part.of the reserve, I think that would be quite satisfactory.
Indians, Nova Scotia-Salaries, $4,400.
What determination has been arrived at regarding the disposition of the Indian Reserve at Sydney? I think this was in the Exchequer Court a year or so ago.

In accordance with the Indian Act, Judge Audette, of the Exchequer Court, went to Sydney, took evidence and completed his report. Under the terms of the Indian Act, this report is to be submitted to the Governor in Council and then to be submitted to Parliament and to be approved or disapproved by resolution at the next ensuing session. I had the privilege of laying the report upon the Table some time ago, and the resolution is now on the Order Paper and will come up in course of time for discussion. It is not my intention to ask any appropriation at this session of Parliament for the purchase of a new reserve. Judge Audette has recommended that the Indians be removed from their present reserve in the town and that another reserve be secured for them, but it is not my intention to ask for any new reserve at the present session.
Has any determination been arrived at as to where the new reserve is to be located?

Three alternative sites have been examined and reported on by Judge Audette. He recommends one of these three; but there has been no determination as to which of the three should be selected, as I thought it somewhat premature, during war time, to vote a sum for this purpose when the matter was not very urgent.
How is the land in the present reserve to be disposed of?
By auction sale.
In regard to the removal of the Sydney reserve, how did it become necessary to invoke the terms of the Act? To what extent did the Indians make objection, and on what grounds?

I was informed that it was by reason of the circumstances connected with this particular reserve that my hon. friend introduced the amendment to the Indian Act in 1911. This reserve is on one of the main thoroughfares in the city of Sydney, which has a population of about 19,000. On several occasions agents of the department interviewed the Indians and endeavoured to get them to make a surrender. The Indians, however, refused to do so, largely on the ground that, as many of them work in the steel plant and the reserve is convenient to their occupations in the city, a change would 'be inconvenient. Some of them are quite agreeable to surrender provided they get another suitable reserve, but they do not wish to be moved any considerable distance from the town.
What was offered the Indians as a consideration for their voluntary removal?

Practically the same considerations and provisions as are offered now by the judge of the Exchequer Court: that we should sell their land to the best possible advantage, move them to another reserve as convenient and suitable as possible, erect their houses on the new reserve, and put them in possession.

As a general rule, when surrenders are taken from the Indians they are guaranteed a minimum valuation on their original property. Is there any such guarantee in this case, and if so, what is the amount?
No. We are to dispose of their present reserve by public auction.
And they are to have no protection in the way of a minimum price?

They would, no doubt,
have the protection of an upset price on the land. We will rehabilitate them in their new reserve and place them under as favourable conditions as possible. We have always endeavoured to protect the rights of the Indians in the past, and shall do so in the future. It is only when they object upon what we consider to be unreasonable grounds that we invoke the terms of the Indian Act. We think they have every guarantee of getting value for their present reserve by our establishing an upset price and disposing of the land by public auction. In a city of that size there would likely be considerable competition for land in the middle of the city and on the main thoroughfare.

As I took some responsibility for placing this amendment in the Indian Act, I am interested in this its first application. While I appreciated at the time the necessity of some such provision, I did not fail to appreciate the right of property held by the Indians in their reserve, and I should be sorry if the minister has not retained that appreciation in his dealings with this Indian band. I know that the circumstances are such as to make it desirable that the Indians should be removed from this reserve, and I appreciate the fact that there may have been difficulties in the way of securing their consent. But when' the strong arm of the law is invoked in dealing with the property of these people and with their personal rights, the Government should take not a less careful but a more careful view of the measure of those rights. They should be sure that nothing is done to derogate from the right of those people to the full value of the property. The property is well known to the public and it must have some measure of fixed value, if city real estate has any fixed value to-day in Canada. The services of the Commissioner should have been utilized to satisfy the Indians and those who wished to see justice done them that they would get a fair value for the land; and the sum so considered to be a fair value should be stated to the Indians as well as to the House. My hon. friend will understand that I make no suggestion of impropriety of action on his part or on the part of any of his officials.
But I can see very grave danger in the fact of the Government simply reaching out its hand and taking away their property from these people and selling it to the highest bidder without giving any assurance to them or t<o the country that they will be absolutely protected. I do not need to go into any further details as to what may occur in such cases, but it will certainly appear right to the minister that he should have availed himself of the services of a commissioner tp place a valuation upon that village.
That has been done.
I have asked the minister for that valuation, and he has not given it to me.

I think the hon. gentleman must have misunderstood me. The commissioner did inquire and take evidence as to the value of the' present reserve, and he has given his estimate of the value. I just forget the amount, but it was some-

where in the neighbourhood of $5,000. The hon. member knows that the reserve consisted of only a little over two acres.
Yes, I am quite aware of that.	.

The commissioner took
evidence from several parties as to the valuation of the land, and he made a recommendation himself as to the value of it.

That, of course, clears the point provided that the department is prepared to stand by that valuation of the commissioner and to guarantee that amount as a minimum to the Indians. That is what I have been arguing for in/ my remarks. Now that the minister has stated the amount, it has become public, and while some may think the amount too small and some too large, unless the amount is fixed and publicly stated, I still mainlain chat the Indians are not receiving fair protection.
I understand the minister has been discussing the Sydney reserve?
Yes.
The minister has made the statement that there are three sites available; where are the sites?

A couple of weeks ago I
laid the report of the judge upon the table of the House. I cannot carry all the details in my memory.

I will look into the matter myself. The minister will recollect that this "subject was brought up a few years ago, and that I suggested to him then that the Indians of the Sydney reserve are in a somewhat different position from the Indians in other parts of the Maritime Provinces. The Indians at Whycocomagh and other reserves are following their ancient occupations of basket-making and tubmaking, but the Indians of Sydney get work around Sydney and they do not follow the old occupations of the Indian tribes in that district. The only interest that I have in the matter, as representing the Indians, is that I should like the minister to take precautions to see that the Indians are not sent so far away from Sydney that they will not be in a position to follow the occupations in which they have been brought up, such as working in the mines or with private families. Apart from that, it would be for the interest of Sydney that the Indians should be removed.
I .do not think there will be any interference with regard to their following their former occupations.
I presume there will be a surplus left out of the $5,000 after paying for the new reserve. What is proposed to be done with that surplus?
My hon. friend means the surplus over and above the $5,000, that is, if we put the land up for sale and it fetches more than $5,000.
Yes.
That would go to the Indians.
Is the amount to be funded for them or distributed amongst the members of the tribe? [DOT]

The hon. member overlooks this fact. We have to secure a new reserve, and the amount received for the land will not be nearly sufficient to place the Indians on a new reserve, and we shall have to come to Parliament for an extra appropriation. The surplus over and above the $5,000 will he applied to the expense of settling the Indians on the new reserve. We shall have to purchase a reserve, have buildings put up, remove the Indians and so on, so that the surplus over the $5,000 will be applied to that.
Indian Department-Miscellaneous and unforeseen, $9,162.
How much of the vote for miscellaneous and unforeseen was expended last year?
Do the officers of my hon. friend's department not know approximately how much of the vote was expended last year?

The deputy informs me that it was nearly all expended.
New Brunswick Indians-Salaries, relief, medical attendance and medicines, miscellaneous and unforeseen, repairs to roads, and to provide for encouragement of agriculture, $16,284.
That is the. same amount as last year.
How many officials are included in the salary item?

There is the superintendent of the northeastern division; there is an agent at Buctouche; there is an agent at Fredericton for the southwestern division;
there is an agent at Perth for the northern division, and then we have constables at Big Cove, Kent County, Burnt Church, Northumberland county and Eel Ground, Northumberland county.
Has the agent at Perth been changed lately?
Mr. Wootten is the agent there.
There was a Mr. Waite there.
He was removed some time ago.	.
For what reason?

The hon. gentleman will remember that either last session or the session before there was some discussion in connection with some timber cutting on the reserve, and as we did not think that Mr. Waite fulfilled all his duties on that occasion, we removed him from his position .

It is very unfortunate that Mr. Waite has been removed froth his position, because if he had remained as agent of the Indian reserve, probably the wood that the minister mentions would be preserved better than ft will be now.
It was during Mr. Waite's regimp that the wood was removed.

Surely the minister does not blame Mr. Waite for cutting timber on the Indian reserve. I know something about the matter, and I do not think the minister ought to make that charge against Mr. Waite, because Mr. Waite did all he could to preserve the Tobique Indian reserve, when a friend of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries went as far as he could go. I want to give the Minister of the Interior credit that when he found out exactly what the condition was, he stopped the cutting of timber. The minister is entitled to a good deal of credit for saving an Indian reserve from the political grafters who are after it. Do not blame Mr. Waite for this.
Is it the intention of the Government to appoint a second superintendent of Indian agencies for the Maritime Provinces9
No.
Is there a special appropriation for repairing the road on the Indian reserve at Edmundston?
Yes.

I hope the grant 'will be sufficient to put this road in good repair, because every spring it is almost impossible to go through that Indian reserve, and as that road is the main highway along the St. John river, I hope the minister will give a good grant so that we shall have a pretty good road in the near future.
There has been some correspondence on that matter.
I should like to know if a certain gentleman by the name of Colonel Sheridan is still in the employ of the department as Indian agent in the .province of New Brunswick.
Yes.

Does the minister remember that about a year ago I pointed out to him that this gentleman had been compelled to resign his seat in the Legislature of New Brunswick for -wrong-doing. I do not want to go into the details again to-night, for I gave them to .the minister a year ago, and the minister was very much surprised, I believe, when he got that information. He promised to investigate the matter, and I think he even went so far as to say that if the facts were as alleged Colonel Sheridan was not.a proper man to occupy a position under the Government. So strong was the feeling against the conduct of this gentleman and his confreres in the county of Kent that at the last provincial election the Conservative majority of 800 was converted into a Liberal majority of 600. In the face of all these facts, will the minister still persist in keeping a man of that stamp in the employ of this Government at a big salary? It seems to me I am putting up a fair proposition. I believe the minister wants to administer the department fairly. I have always had the most courteous treatment from him, and have always found him disposed to do what is right and fair, and I therefore cannot understand how he can continue to employ this man in view of the very distressing circumstances which I pointed out to him last year.

I remember the hon. gentleman bringing to my attention certain statements of his own about Colonel Sheridan; I had never heard of the circumstances before, and I promised to make an inquiry. I looked up the judge's report, and if I recollect aright Colonel Sheridan was censured by the judge who tried the case for certain indiscretions. I think certain work had been done in the name of his son.
The trouble is that the work was not done, but his son drew the pay for it. Names were added to the pay list and the money was paid to Colonel Sheridan.	.

I understand that certain small amounts were paid. I knew nothing of the circumstances when I appointed Colonel Sheridan, and after looking into the circumstances related by my hon. friend, I did not think Colonel Sheridan had been guilty of impropriety such as would warrant me in dismissing him, as he was carrying out his duties as Indian Agent quite properly.

Does the minister think that a man who was not fit to sit in the legislature of New Brunswick, because of irregular practices, itf a perfectly fit and proper person to act as Indian Agent in his department?
I do not know whether he was fit to sit in the legislature or not.
He got out.
Lots of men get out.

I am sorry for the minister. I want to say here publicly that I spoke to the minister about the raid on the timber on the Tobique reserve, and the minister did everything a minister of the Crown could be expected to do. I want to give him credit publicly for saving that reserve to the Indians, but I am sorry, after he has done so well in that respect, to see him allowing this condition of affairs to exist in another , part of the province.
I am sorry my colleague from New Brunswick is not in his place", because he is better acquainted with the circumstances. I know he has a different idea from my hon. friend.
I think the minister's colleague is very glad indeed that he was temporarily called out of the Chamber.
I was not in the House when the Quebec vote for the Indians was passed. Was any road-making done on the Maria and Restigouche reserves last year, and is any contemplated for the coming summer?
Work was done last year, and we intend to do work on both reserves this summer.	[DOT]
How much work was done last year, and how much will be done this summer?
$500 was expended on each reserve last year, and we expect to spend about the same amount this year.

Will that complete the
work that is contemplated?
Mr." ROCHE:	We usually spread the
work over a series of years,
Who is in charge of the work?
Nobody has been appointed for the work this summer.

Is the work being done
by day labour?	[DOT]
Yes, I can get the foreman's name for my hon. friend later on.
Are Indians employed in this work, or any body at all? [DOT]
We give Indians the preference.
Were any Indians employed on these reserves?
That is my impression.
Who is the medical officer in charge of the Restigouche Reserve?
Dr. Martin. -
Who is the medical officer in charge of the Maria Reserve?
Dr. Boileau.	'
Do they receive a salary, or are they paid fees?

Dr. Boileau receives $300
per annum. Dr. Martin is paid on account and receives no stipulated salary.

Have any requests been
made for seed grain to increase the grain production on the Restigouche Reserve? A petition was sent here some time ago asking that the Reserve be fenced in, so that the Indians could go in for more extensive production,
They made a request, and their request has been granted.
To what extent?

Whatever they asked for
was granted. I think it was in the neighbourhood of $500.
Do you buy the grain?
The agent buys the grain.

Does he purchase from
the Government or anywhere he likes?
He has a free hand.

Has the minister received any complaints from the band at Woodstock, New Brunswick, that they were not being treated fairly in the distribution of supplies? I have always had very grave doubts of the wisdom of the policy of sup. plying the Indians with a few 'pounds of pork or flour, but it has been the custom ever since. Confederation, and I am not going to raise that question now.
I know that a great deal of fault is found with the giving of supplies, on the ground that the Indian is not treated fairly. I do not know whether that is true or not, but I know that representations to that effect have been made to the department. The charge is that when the Indian wants supplies he must go to a certain store with his order for two dollars, five dollars, or whatever it may be. The storekeeper, they complain, gives them some things, but will not give them others. The information I get is that they could not get pork or flour, but could get other things that they do not want. Also, they claim that they are charged such exorbitant prices that their order only lasts for a few minutes. I do not make any charge, but I draw the matter to the attention of the minister without mentioning names. Has he made an investigation, and if so, what is the result?

Complaints have been made along the lines indicated by the hon. member (Mr. Carvell). The deputy minister instructed the inspector to investigate these charges and this was done. The report of the inspector was favourable to the action of the agent, and showed that there was comparatively little in the charges.

Were the Indians given an opportunity to be heard, or was the investigation an ex parte one? If an investigation was ever held in which the Indians were allowed to be represented, I have not heard of it, and I may tell the minister that an investigation purely ex parte, under the conditions existing in New Brunswick to-day in his department, would be of little use. I did a little investigating myself, and came to the conclusion that there was reason to believe that the Indians were justified in the position they took. It is for that reason I bring the matter to the minister's attention. I certainly do not want to do injustice to anybody; I am making no charges, but there was sufficient evidence to satisfy me that there ought to be either a change of merchants or a change in procedure of supplying goods to the Indians.
My information is that the Indians were afforded an opportunity to give evidence. I will send the hon. gentleman a copy of the report.
And will the minister please send, also, a copy of the evidence on which the report is based?
With regard to the Resti-gouche reserve, has any application been made to secure any part of that reserve as a pulpwood limit and mill site?
No.
Has there been any move in that direction?
No.

I understand that the
province of New Brunswick will spend some money on the Indian reserve at Edmunds-ton, and so will the Department of the Interior. Has the minister named a person to supervise the work? And, if so, has he appointed the commissioner of the parish, or has he appointed the commissioner from Edmundston, near which the land is situated?
We have not named anyone.

Is it the intention of
the Government to employ either of the men I have suggested, or will somebody else be appointed?

That point has not been
under consideration as yet, the money for the year not having been voted.

I hope the minister
will take into consideration the appointment either of the commissioner for the town of Edmundston or the commissioner for the parish of St. Basil. I know them both, and both are good men.

I was not in my place
when the Indian Estimates for Ontario were going through. May I be permitted to ask if the minister will let me have the tenders for the sale of timber on the Shawgnaga reserve in January, 1917, and the prices at which the timber was sold?
I will get that information.
Is the same method followed in regard to the Indians of the Quebec reserves as with the Indians of the New Brunswick reserves in the matter of supplies? Is an Indian given an order for [DOT]supplies?
The Indian is not handed the money to go and buy wherever he likes, but the agent directs where the supplies are to be purchased.
Are the charges for goods sold to the Indians supervised by the department?
Yes.
The purchases for the Restigouche reserve would have to be made in Campbellton, N.B.?
Yes.
How many Indian reserves are there in New Brunswick?
Twenty-six.
Is one located at Dorchester?
Yes.

The number of Indians there is very small, and I did not know whether it was a regular reserve, or whether the Indians had dropped in there themselves and were being looked after more or less by the agents in the province of New Brunswick? Following up what has been said by the hon. member for Oarleton (Mr. Carvell), I may say that from what I have been able to learn [DOT] with regard to supplies furnished to Indians in my own county, no check at all seems to be kept. There may be a telephone message purporting to come from the Indian agent at some distance away, and on that authority supplies may be taken to the camp for the Indians. But there seems to be no check, the agent himself does not know what is actually supplied except as he is informed by those who furnish the supplies. The appropriation for this purpose for the province of New Brunswick is small, but for the whole country the aggregate is a very considerable one, and as this is a business matter, one would think that businesslike care should be exercised to have some check on the goods supplied, and the prices charged.
Some, of course, do such work as the loading of vessels in the harbour in that locality. We can understand that complaints might readily be made by those people when there are perhaps not very good grounds for them but I do know that the supplying of the Indians is done in a most 'offhand way by telephone message, or something of that kind, the goods are taken to the camp and nobody knows anything more about them till somebody sends a bill.

We must have confidence in the agent and he certifies to these ac-

counts before they come to the department. We depend on his business capacity and honesty to see that these are proper accounts. I could quite well understand that if he was 25 miles away from the Indians who were going to be supplied he could not be present to check over the supplies and he would have to telephone to place the order. But, he is supposed, in the discharge of his duties, to see that the Indians are not imposed upon. If the hon. gentleman has information with regard to some individual Indians, or if he knows the Indian character well enough, he will know that they are not at all averse to putting up a kick occasionally and that if there is any ground, and sometimes if there is none at all, they grumble. But, we do trust to the reliability of our agents to see that they are not imposed upon.

I quite understand that the complaints of a very large class of them would have to be taken more or less with a grain of salt. But, we have an agent who has charge of the reserves in my county who lives not 20 miles away from the reserve but possibly 60 or 70 miles away. There are places in Westmorland where there will be only four or five families of Indians. I did not know whether they were regular Indian reserves or not or whether they were just small communities. At Dorchester there are only a few families and yet I understand, it is a regular Indian reserve. The minister says that the agent must certify to the accounts. Anybody who knows the conditions at all knows that when the agent certifies to the accounts he has no more information about these accounts than the minister has himself. These matters are small but I think it would be well to reorganize the system down there and have somebody in the different localities to see that the goods that are purchased for the Indian tribes are properly supplied and that they get value for the money paid. We should have some assurance that the goods are supplied at fair and reasonable prices. The agent has no information in regard to these matters that would enable him to certify to the accuracy of the accounts and he simply accepts the accounts from the merchants and those who supply the goods. These merchants might as well send the accounts direct to the department and do away with the agent altogether because he is absolutely of no use.
What would the hon. gentleman suggest?
I would suggest that, rather than have an agent there who does not know the value of the goods supplied, the merchants should send their accounts direct to the department.
The only thing about that is that the Auditor General could not pass them.

Unless you adopt some
special plan to get around the Auditor General, I suppose we cannot expect anything else. But, I speak seriously about this matter. There is no one who has sufficient knowledge to certify to these accounts, and it is a matter of leaving the merchants to supply the goods to the different reserves. Whether they supply the goods or not they charge for them and they are paid.

I was not in the House when the Nova Scotia items were up, and if you will pardon me, Mr. Chairman, for a moment, I would like to refer to a few little things appertaining to the Nova Scotia vote which has just been passed. Near the town where I live we have a small colony of Indians. They have no reserve and no land. There are a few 9 p.m. families, numbering about 20 or something like that. They have been living on the same land, I suppose, for forty years. It is only through the kindness and generosity of the people who own the land that they are permitted to reside on it. Some day these people will turn them off, I suppose. Often, in the old days before this Government came into power, I used, to speak to my hon. friend's predecessor, the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs about this matter, but I could not get anything done. I think the Indians should be taken away altogether and put with the Indians at Sydney, or some other provision made for them. There is no agent or doctor there. The doctor at Sydney is the nearest doctor, and at a certain season of the year he has to go 17 miles to reach them. In the summer time there is a ferry and it is only five miles. But in the winter time, when the Indians would be likely to require the services, of a doctor, the nearest doctor would be 17 miles away. The same care should be taken of this little colony as is taken of Indians in other parts. The land on which they live is not valuable land and it would not be expensive to get a few acres for them where they are so that they would be on their own property. I realise



that it would be very difficult to get them to give up the place because they have become attached to- the spot where they have been living for -forty or, perhaps, fifty years. But they never had any organization or anything done for them.
I also want to say a word about the Sydney Indians. I have lived in Sydney for many years and I know many of these Indians -personally. I took a great deal of interest in the report that I saw had been made with regard to their removal. I would suggest to the minister that instead of selling this land, for which he might get a few thousand dollars, he should give it to the city. We will call it Roche Park and it will commemorate the minister for all time to come. Sydney is quite a large city and in that end of the town where the reserve is located there is no land available for park purposes. It is right on the seashore, and it is valuable property for a park. It is outside of the commercial part of the city. I presume the water front is still the property of the Government, and it could be made a beauty spot and would be of great value to the city and people generally. The ordinary man in Sydney, with his wife and children, having the privilege of visiting that park, going to the shore and enjoying the magnificent bathing place there, would bless the memory of the minister if he made that reserve into a small public park. The money that he would get for it is a mere bagatelle and would soon be forgotten. To give this land to the city as a park would be an excellent and generous thing to do. Victoria Park, at the other end of the city, was practically given to the city for park purposes by the Imperial Government. It was Admiralty ground in the time when the island of Cape Breton was a province and Sydney was a garrison city. That park has been beautified by the city. About a mile And a half awray to the south is this little bit of land occupied by the Indians, and it is rather a drawback to that part of the city. The Indians themselves would be better off elsewhere. I would suggest that it would be better not to hand the money to be paid to the Indians for this land direct to them, but rather to place it in the hands of trustees, such as the Indian agent, who is a very capable man, and Reverend Pather McAdam, the priest there, who has been very kind to the Indians. In this way the money would be paid to the Indians at intervals when they needed it, whereas if it were given to them direct they would spend it very quickly and in a way which would not be to their own advantage.

I would suggest also that the small settlement of Indians who have really squatted in the town of North Sydney should be removed. They occupy land really by the grace of the owners, and have been there for about thirty years. I know that it will be difficult to get them to stay in any other place as the Indian is peculiar in that way.

When I said that any surplus over the estimate of $5,000 would be handed to the Indians, I overlooked the fact- that there would not likely be any surplus as it would cost a good deal more than $5,000 to secure a reserve for the Indians elsewhere. As to the suggestion that this land should be handed over to the city of Sydney for park purposes, I do not wash to say anything to prejudice the proposal, but this is the first time it has been made. The city of Sydney seems to be rather apathetic on the whole question; I do not think that any of the municipal officials even appeared before Judge Audette. It has been the intention, if possible, to place the Indians at North Sydney on the same reserve with those from Sydney when a new reserve is obtained.

What is the result of the work of the commission?

The commission ceased
their labours last July, and under the terms of the Order in Council appointing them, they were to make a report to the provincial government and to the Dominion Government, which report was to be adopted by the two governments prior to its being submitted to Parliament. The report was furnished just about the time that the old government in British Columbia weTe in the midst of an election campaign, and they were too busy with other matters to deal with this report. The new government, since it has come into power, has been busily occupied; it has held its first session of Parliament. We have had some communications with the prime minister of British Columbia to "try to expedite the consideration of the report in order that we might have the matter taken up and action taken at this session. Mr. Brewster stated that he was far too busy to give the report his attention during the session of Parliament, but that he would have it taken up as expeditiously as possible and have it dealt with. We are awaiting the action of the British Columbia Government before taking any further proceedings prior to laying the report upon the table of the House.
What was the purpose to be achieved by this somewhat luxurious commission?

The hon. gentleman knows that the question of Indian reserves in British Columfbia has been a great bone of contention between the Indians, the provincial government, and the Dominion Government for many years past, and this commission was appointed with a view to clearing up all these difficulties. It was claimed by the Indians that they were not in possession of sufficient land for their purposes, and the contention was made by the British Columbia Government that in many instances there was far too much land for the number of Indians, and in order to do away with those conflicting representations it was decided to have this commission investigate each reserve. That was done very thoroughly, and I believe a very excellent report was made. The country is mountainous and very extensive, and many reserves are difficult of access. The commission visited each reserve personally and that meant a great deal of time. They took evidence of all the Indians interested, and they have made recommendations that those reserves in which it was found that there was too much land for the Indians to occupy should be cut down to what the commission considered to be the requisite area, and in other reserves where they considered the land was too small" in area for a reserve they have recommended that additions be made. It was with the reserves alone that this commission was occupied, and while I am not at liberty to divulge the nature of the report, because it is a very voluminous and exhaustive document, I believe they have made a most excellent report and one which I trust will commend itself to all parties concerned. From what little conversation I have had with the Premier of British Columbia in regard to the matter, I am inclined to think there will not be much difficulty in having his government approve the report, and if that is the case I am satisfied, from my slight perusal of portions of the report, that it should recommend itself to the Dominion Government as well. I cannot go into the details of the recommendations, because there is a separate report on each reserve, but the recommendations were along the lines I have indicated.
When was the commission appointed?
I think in 1913. I was in the Old Country at the time the commission was appointed.
What was the total bill?
The total bill, including salaries, travelling and all other expenses, amounted to $316,782, of which the province of British Columbia bears one half.
Did the closing of the work of the commission and the change of government in British Columbia merely synchronize, or had one any bearing on the other?	.
I would not venture an opinion on that.

Five.
The report would need to be good seeing that it cost over $300,000.
Has the report been printed?
Yes, but under the terms of the Order in Council appointing the commission, the report has to be approved by both governments before it can be laid on the Table.
Laying it on the Table will be merely a matter of form, as the subject has already been settled before it comes to the consideration of this Parliament.

It is not a mere matter of form. The people's representatives have a perfect right to criticise the report and to see how the money was expended, but we are not permitted to lay the report on the Table until it has been endorsed by the two governments.

That means that an effective criticism by Parliament would be the defeat of the Government. That seems to be going o.utside altogether of parliamentary procedure. It is taking the control of affairs out of the hands of Parliament very effectively. I think the conditions surrounding the- issue of the commission are nearly as remarkable as the expenditure on its behalf.

I think it is a most fortunate thing for this Dominion of Canada that the Government of British Columbia changed. This arrangement seems to have been a deal between the Government of British Columbia alid the Dominion Government to divide up, as they saw fit, certain valuable assets belonging either to the Indians or to the province of British Columbia, and charging the expense to the province and the Dominion without regard to the Parliament of the Dominion or the legislature of the province. As/a specimen of autocratic government and disregard of the rights of the people and of their representatives, I think that stands absolutely in a class by itself.

the arbitrators did. That is the reason we are not satisfied with the award, and we have appealed it to the judge. There is some difference
in the figures. This Kitsilano Indian reserve was presumably the property .of the Indians. It was under the jurisdiction and administration of my hon. friend (Mr. Roche). While it was under his jurisdiction and administration, some person or perspns presumably acting for the Government of British Columbia, without let or hindrance from the minister so far as we know, went in and made arrangements with the Indians under which the Indians were paid $216,000, and they vacated the reserve. There never was such a case in all the history of Canada before-that the Government of the Dominion neglected to exercise that jurisdiction and assume that responsibility that properly rested upon their shoulders for the protection of the interests of the Indians. They allowed the Indians to be dickered with by these agents, more or less responsible; they allowed them to be removed from the reserve; they allowed their buildings to be burned; and they allowed the Government of British Columbia, I believe, or the hirelings pi that Government, to assume jurisdiction over that reserve as though it were their property and not the property of the Indians or under the jurisdiction of my hon. friend. I do not know whether I said at the time, but I say now -but, perhaps I am wrong in suggesting that this was under the jurisdiction of my hon, friend; I believe the undertaking originated under his predecessor-that I am unable to conceive that this conjunction of circumstances could have taken place without a definite understanding between the
gentleman, whoever he was, then at the head of the Indian Department of the Dominion of Canada, and those who directed the affairs of the province of British Columbia, and interesting themselves in these transactions. What their purpose may have been I am not here to say, but I know what the purpose of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs ought to have been, and that was to secure the Indians their rights and the full extent of those rights. Anything else than this was a dereliction of duty, and was a reflection on the good faith of the Dominion of Canada and behind the Dominion of Canada on the good faith of the British Crown. There were other moneys paid besides those paid to the Indians. I do not know whether the amount my hon. friend has stated to me is the total amount that was paid by the Government of British Columbia, but some money was paid to the Indians, and some was paid to friends of that Government, because these moneys afterwards became the subject of a lawsuit, and so of public record. Were the amounts so paid outside of what was paid to the Indians included in this $216,000?
I understand that moneys were paid by the British Columbia government, by way of commissions that were unwarranted. These are not included in the $216,000.

Was the amount about
$100,000?
I do not know.

My recollection is that
the amount was in the neighbourhood of $80,000. That would bring the tojal payments of the British Columbia Government to about $300,000, of which the Indians received $216,000, and the friends of the British Columbia Government, $80,000. This feature makes the transaction even more remarkable than it was in the beginning. Does this $216,000 include the expenses of removing the Indians as well as the cash payments made to them?	,
Only the cash payments.

So that besides the $216,000 there were the removal expenses and the commissions. All this money was paid, and all this transaction was entered into, either with or without the knowledge and consent of this Government through its then Superintendent General of Indian Affairs. If this transaction went on without the

knowledge of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, then he was so utterly negligent of his duty that he should be condemned; and if it went on with his knowledge, there is no other possible suggestion that that he was a party to the transaction for reasons other than the public good or the benefit of the Indians. The Indians owned that property. If there was any question as to their ownership, it was certainly not the business of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs to question that right; it was his business to maintain that right, to maintain it to the limit of his powers under the law. But instead of doing that he did not even exercise the ordinary supervision that his duty requires him to exercise, to prevent unlawful access to the reserve, unlawful trespass upon it, the unlawful destruction of property of the Indians upon it, and the improper and unlawful transactions with the Indians concerned.
There is no way in which the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs can justify his position in connection with this transaction. The Government of British Columbia, so my hon. friend says, went into this transaction. They put up this $216,000, they put up the moving expenses and they put up the commission. Why did they do it? Was it the Government that did it, or was it the members of the Government that did it, using the treasury of the province to enable them to do it? However, the transaction went on, and whether it wa* the exposure made in the House of Com mons, or whether it may have been protests made on the Pacific coast, for some reason or other apparently it did not go through as intended. Now, the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, who was asleep at the switch when these transactions were going on, has awakened. He is now doing business. He now claims that the Indians own the reserve and he is proposing to deal with the Harbour Commissioners of Vancouver for its sale. I think I remember that when this matter was considered before, my hon, friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) had bright hopes that this reserve was going to 'be made a present of to Vancouver, or that in some way Vancouver was to benefit immensely out of these transactions, in which the Government of British Columbia was the chief actor, and to which the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs was a consenting party. Apparently these bright hopes of my hon. friend have been shattered.
My hon. friend is again in error.
Did not my hon. friend entertain such hopes?
No, my hon. friend is entirely and absolutely wrong in his idea.

Thank you. The present that the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs purposes not to hand, to the city of Vancouver is the difference between $350,000, say, and $1,250,000, a difference of about $900,000. That certainly would be sufficient to make the citizens of Vancouver sit up and take notice and greet with enthusiasm the action of the late Government of British Columbia and the support that my hon. friend gave it in the House when the matter was up.

My hon. friend is again
mistaken.

It seems strange that,
when the fall of the Government has occurred in British Columbia and when a king has arisen there who knows not Joseph, the price of this reserve suddenly rises from a little over $300,000, paid to the Indians, paid for their transportation and paid for commissions that were the subject of a lawsuit, to which figure the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs at that day must have consented, to the figure of $1,250,000.
