Certainly. Do you think that has anything to do with it?

Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has, by a series of rather cleverly constructed statements, sought to involve the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs of the Federal Government in a transaction which he knows perfectly well has nothing whatever to do with this department. I have had a very close knowledge of this matter from the very commencement, and I wish to state that the greatest credit is due to the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs for the firm stand he has taken on this question from the beginning. The facts of the case are very different from the impression conveyed by the hon. member for Edmonton, and. I am surprised that he, with the opportunities he has had during the last three years of ascertaining the facts, should attempt to make the cheapest kind of political capital out of a question which reflects only credit upon this Government, whatever may be his estimate of the action of the provincial government of British Columbia.
The facts are briefly something along this line:	About four years ago, the provincial
government, as a result of a general feeling in the city of Vancouver that this reserve should be utilized for other purposes than that of an Indian reserve, undertook to get possession of it from the Indians. In order that the House may have a correct view of the situation, they should know the location of this reserve. My hon. friend from Edmonton knows perfectly well where the reserve is situated, practically in the heart of the city, at the mouth of False creek, in a very important and strategic point in the harbour.

I do not like to interrput my hon. friend, but I should like him to keep a little closer to the line. My hon. friend is hardly correct in saying this reserve is situated in the heart of the city. It is well situated, but it is not in the heart of the city.
It is in the heart of the city.

It may be in the heart
of the city geographically, but it is not in the business centre.
It is in the heart of the business centre.

In the heart of the
future city.
My hon. friend is not correct. I know what I am speaking about; it is within half a mile of the Vancouver hotel.
Across False creek.

And there is three miles of solidly constructed property in each direction from it except on the water side, both west and south. It is right on False Creek which is a hive of industry. During the past five, six, seven or eight years, there has been a tonnage of from three to five million tons of coastwise trade in and out of False Creek, starting at a point immediately adjoining the reserve and up the creek, and immediately across within 100 yards of the reserve on the other side. False Creek, of course, is a little arm of the sea, about two miles in length. It is a perfect hive of industry, and that is where the Kitsilano Indian reserve is. My hon. friend sought to lead the House to believe that the provincial government went on the reserve and in some subtle manner induced the Indians to leave, and then burned their houses and arbitrarily took possession. That is not the fact. My hon. friend knows it, or ought to know it. The Kitsilano Indian reserve was never a reserve of residents. It belongs to certain bands of Indians, part of the Squamish tribe. They live chiefly on the Capilano Indian reserve across the inlet, some miles away. They came to False Creek and Kitsilano occasionally, landed with their fishing boats, and went up to the city to make purchases, as they used to land at the old slip at the foot of Gore avenue. Indians generally have some one place where they land. On the reserve were a couple of old shacks, you would scarcely call them shacks, simply a few poles put up with a few old boards to keep them together, and occasionally the Indians used to stay there overnight, to no good purpose for themselves or the community. I think my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) generally speaking, desires to be honest in his criticism, but in this case I think he has departed from his usual course. He knows perfectly well that there is no greater curse to the Indians of Canada than these reserves situated in the heart of a thickly populated community like Vancouver and some other cities in the West where Indians can come in and are subject to the evil influences of a closely settled city district. That is one of the problems with which the Assistant Super-

intendent General of Indian Affairs is constantly faced. It was exceedingly desirable that this reserve should be turned into	useful	industrial property and the Indians properly compensated. When my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) was Superintendent General of Indian Affairs he was asked by the city of Vancouver time and time again, and he'* knows that the candidate representing the party which he represented in this House, on the hustings in Vancouver, promised the people of Vancouver that if returned to power his Government, that is the late Government, would make a present of this reserve to the people of Vancouver. That was one of the baits held out to the people of Vancouver. The statement of my hon. friend that I* bad made such suggestions is absolutely without foundation. Not only did I never make that statement, but I have always held, as my correspondence on the records of the department will show, that the Indians should be properly compensated for that property and that any transfer should be under the direction and control of the Indian Department. But here is what occurred. The old provincial government, knowing the sentiment of Vancouver desired to get rid of the Indians on the Kitsilano Indian reserve. They took the ground that they had a reversionary right, and that if the Indians left the reserve and abandoned it the reserve reverted to the province. But, fouT years ago, the moment I heard that action was being contemplated by the provincial government, I took the view that they had no such right and that the reversionary right as such did not exist. I lwld that view to-day. I placed that view before the department who at once took cognizance of it, and the Prime Minister, on the floor of the old House of Commons, the first time it was brought to his attention, stated that this Government, under his leadership, had given no authority to the provincial government to take the action which they did.
Moreover, he stated on that occasion and on several occasions since that this Government had never recognized the right of the province to take the action that they did. Agents of the provincial government induced the Indians to accept $216,000 and $1,500 for the removal of some dead bodies which were taken to another reserve. The Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, the Assistant Superintendent General of Indian Affairs and I myself hold that the provincial government had not acted according to law, or according to their rights,
and the action was never recognized by this Government. This Government deserves from my hon. friend not condemnation, but credit.
My hon. friend states that this Government stood aside and allowed the provincial government to take possession and remain in possession of that reserve. The provincial government had never been properly in possession of that reserve. My hon. friend infers that the Harbour Commissioners dealt with the provincial government or with some other authorities for the purchase of this reserve. This is what occurred. The Harbour Commissioners, recognizing the value of this reserve for harbour purposes, and acting under the authority of their Act of incorporation, expropriated the reserve. How did they expropriate it? They offered this Government $500,000 for the reserve about two years ago, but the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs refused the offer on the ground that the amount was not sufficient. They then notified this Government that they intended to take proceedings to expropriate. It was necessary to get the consent of the Government. The Government consented, and a board of arbitration was appointed, consisting of Mr. C. E. Mahon, alderman of the city of Vancouver; Mr. Boreland, a prominent citizen of about 25 years' standing in that city, and Mr. Pound, a gentleman of the highest standing in Vancouver on arbitration matters concerning real estate.	Mr. Pound, by the way, is
treasurer of the Liberal Association in the city of Vancouver-and he is a gentleman from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head. This board was appointed bfifore the election last fall, so there can be no suggestion of political influence. They sat in arbitration for some months, after which they adjourned because Mr.. Livingstone, representing the Indians and the Crown, had to attend Supreme Court in the East. Their finding, which was brought down, if I remember rightly, in January of this year, was that the reservation was worth the sum of $666,000. My hon. friend seeks to make capital out of this. He says that the Government allowed the reserve to be sold in boom times for $216,000, which is absolutely without foundation in fact. This Government not only opposed the action, but prevented it as far as it was able. Then, he says, in a time of collapse, the board of arbitration found that the property was worth $666,000. The facts in that regard are these: the board of arbitration, as by law they were
What is my hon. friend's opinion as to who owns the foreshore?
The Crown, represented by the Dominion Government. That has been decided in this particular case.
Then if it has been decided in this case, the Indians cannot own it.
The question was decided as between the right of the Crown as represented by the province and the right of the Crown as represented by the Dominion.
When?
A couple of years ago; I cannot remember the date.

I understand that the British Columbia Government has always contended that the foreshore of a harbour which at the time the province entered Confederation was not actually used for the purposes of a public harbour and on which no public improvements had been made, would vest in the province. Then the question as to whether the Indians own or not would depend on their title. Some Indians own to low water and some to high water.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Privy Council decided that if a harbour was a public harbour at the time of Confederation, the foreshore is the property of the Crown as represented by the Federal Government.

When I was a member of the late Government and Sir Richard McBride was premier of British Columbia, his Government, when Prince Rupert was established, claimed all the foreshore in the harbour of Prince Rupert.

A case was taken to the Privy Council concerning part of the bed of False Creek, which is connected with this reservation, and it was definitely decided that the foreshore was in the right of the Crown as represented by the Dominion Government.
Could my hon. friend give me the name of the case?

No, but I will tell my
hon. friend how the question rose. My hon. friend gave a piece of property, eighteen acres in extent, in False Creek, to Mr. John Hendry, one of his friends in Vancouver, for ten dollars an acre. Mt. John Hendry, two years afterwards, sold that property to the British Columbia Electric for $700,000. That is where the property lies which was decided by the Privy Council-

I have no recollection
of giving Mr. Hendry any land whatever. As a matter of fact, the rule of the department and the course of practice governing the Marine and Fisheries Department and the Public Works Department ever since Confederation have been to give, at a comparatively nominal rental, leases of the foreshore to people who actually had the riparian rights; but I have no recollection whatever of giving Mr. John Hendry any such land.

I can bring the papers
down to-morrow if my hon. friend so desires. My hon, friend not only gave this property to Mr. John Hendry, but, to give another illustration, he gave to Mr. Robert Kelly and Mr. McFeely for $3,600 a very large piece of property which was refused to a Mr. J. B. Tiffin who owned the foreshore, and that piece was, through the Exchequer Court, sold to this Government for about $360,000.
Would that be the piece of land which was sold by agents who obtained a very large commission on the sale to this Government?
No, it was sold by my hon. friend and his Government to Mr. Robert Kelly and Mr. McFeely, one an eminent Liberal gentleman in Vancouver.
For how much money?

As my hon. friend has
diverted my attention to this matter, I will just digress in order to explain the transaction a little further. I am delighted to have the opportunity. My hon. friend year after year refused to give to Mr. J. B. Tiffin, who owned the Red Cedar lumber mill at that point, a lease of the foreshore. Mr. Tiffin had to sell that property and did sell it to the hon. gentleman's friends, and those gentlemen came down here and within about two months got that property for about one-tenth of its value. I do not wish to digress any further.
I would be glad if my hon. friend would give the facts and not draw on his imagination.

I am not drawing- on
my imagination.
Just a moment. Does my hon. friend say that the same property that was sold to those people for $3,600 was bought back by the present Government for $360,000?

I do say it, and I say it was bought back through the Exchequer Court. There was another very valuable piece of property at the sugar refinery that perhaps my hon. friend will remember. It consisted of some 3,000 feet, and about one-tenth of that property that was sold or given away for $4,000 was leased a couple of years ago for three times the amount for which my hon. friend gave it away. Not once since this Government came into office has any Crown grant been given, but simply leases are given, except when a piece
of property has been occupied for twenty years or more for industrial purposes, and then grants are given on a valuation very much in advance of anything that my hon. friend ever thought of securing.
My hon. friend thought to divert my attention from the real question before the House, and I will now return to that question. The whole question is whether the Indians have the ownership of that foreshore. The Superintendent General of Indian Affairs fixes his valuation on the assumption that they did; the arbitrators went into the matter very carefully, and they decided that the ownership ceased at high-tide mark, and that from there on the Indians had riparian rights, and the amount of $666,000 has been fixed on that basis and premises. The Superintendent General still persists in his protection of the Indians' rights; he still persists in his valuation; he has appealed from the decision of these three estimable and able gentlemen to the Supreme Court of Canada, and the case is before that court at the present time and will be decided as to the matters of law, ownership and value.
So much for this valuation. This is the point I wish to make, that I think my hon. friend from Edmonton has done a grave injustice to the Superintendent General. From the very outset of this transaction there has never been one moment that the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs has not exercised care and solicitude for the rights of the Indians. My hon. friend asked what was to be done with the money, and the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs answered him partially, if not fully. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that the Indian Act provided that half of the money derived from the sale of Indian property is usually given to the Indians and the other half is placed in a fund and kept at Ottawa for the benefit of the Indians. That is exactly what the Superintendent General intends to do when this award is completed; he intends that the money shall go entirely to the use of the Indians.
Let me turn for a moment to the Indians themselves and to their action. The Indian accepted $216,000 for their interest in this reserve, and this amount was divided up amongst about twenty Indians. These Indians are satisfied with what they have received and they have given up all their rights. My hon. friend, naturally, in his endeavour to make a little political capital, tried to involve the Superintendent General in that transaction, and he said this: By the very fact that the provincial Govern-

ment paid those Indians, the Superintendent General must have been a party to the transaction, and in some way or another, his friends benefited from it. That did not follow at all. I hold, and the Superintendent General holds that the provincial Government had no right to carry out that transaction, but the provincial government claimed-and they have some ground on which to base their claim-that they own these reserves the minute they are abandoned by the Indians, and they went to the Indians and asked them if they wanted to abandon this reserve. The Indians replied that they did; the amount was agreed upon, and the reserve was abandoned by the Indians voluntarily. The Indians were not put off the reserve; they went off it willingly, and the provincial authorities then said: This reserve is ours. I have explained to my hon. friend my reasons for saying that the provincial Government was wrong. The Indian is a ward of the Dominion Government; he is in exactly the same position as a minor, as a child under twenty-one years of age, and that child or that minor has no right to abandon a piece of property that belongs to him without the consent of his guardian, and therefore I think the position of the Dominion authorities is sound, and the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs was perfectly right in taking the stand that the provincial transaction was not sound nor right. The question now arises: Is it fair to reimburse the provincial government? I contend that it is right to do so, because if you do not, you will pay the Indians an additional sum. It is quite true that after all, we cannot ignore what the provincial government did. We may say to them: You have spent your money; you had no right to give it to the Indians; go and get it bdck from them. I suppose that could be done, but that is not a proper view to take of the matter. The Dominion Government naturally say that they are prepared to reimburse the provincial government for such rights as they may establish, and those rights will be established by fair arbitration, I presume by some independent arbitrator such as a Supreme Court judge, or an Exchequer Court judge, or some other authority agreed on between the two parties. I think that fairly well explains the situation. In my opinion, the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, as representing the Dominion Government, has acted in good faith, and he deserves credit for safeguarding the rights of those Indians.

I would not have detained the cominitte but for the extraordinary statement which my hon. frieqd seemed to think it was necessary to make in regard to the action of the department over which I presided for some few years, in regard tp a piece of property at the city of Vancouver. The matters to which he has referred have nothing whatever to do with the question under discussion, but thinking in some way to discredit the management of my department the hon. gentleman has stated that I practically gave away the foreshore rights in the city of Vancouver to friends, which foreshore rights were pf very considerable value. It is nearly six year3 since I was minister, and I do not recall any of the eases to which my hon. friend refers. But I do know that ever since Confederation there has been a rule in the department that in respect to foreshore privileges leases will be given at almost a nominal rental to the riparian owners for the purpose of making improvements to the property, by way of erecting wharves, factories or other buildings. That was the rule long before I came into Parliament, and I have no doubt it is the rule followed by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The leases are given by Order in Council on the joint report of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the Minister of Public Works.

I think the matter is
always initiated in the Department pf Marine and Fisheries. The valuation whether rental or purchase price is fixed by that department, and not by the Department of Public Works. Then the engineer of the Department of Public Works reports whether there would be any objection from the public standpoint, whether there wpuld be any obstruction to" navigation, and so forth.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is a report from the engineer of the Department of Marine and Fisheries that it would not interfere with navigation, and a report from the engineer of Public Works that the property is not required for public purposes. [DOT]
I think the minister will agree that the valuation is fixed toy the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and therefore my hon. friend from Vancouver is barking up the wrong tree.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do net say the valuation is actually fixed by the Department of ' Marine and Fisheries. The report is signed

by both ministers, but the matter certainly initiates in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Then it goes to the Minister of Public Works, and if he approves he joins in the report; so both ministers agree.

But the signature of
the Minieter of Public. Works is of a more formal character. He simply has to decide whether the property is required for public purposes. The matter always originates with the Department of Marine and Fisheries, which fixes the valuation. That was the practice when I was minister; it has been the practice ever since Confederation, and I have no doubt it is the practice to-day. So my hon. friend is barking up the wrong tree when he attacks me for making an arrangement with regard to the rental at which the foreshore rights in Vancouver City should foe leased. It is a perfectly simple matter. The riparian owner, having land fronting on navigable water, can prevent any obstruction being erected which would in any way interfere with his access. He can have approach to his land by steamer, scow or any other vessel which can navigate to it. No person would be allowed to erect an obstruction in front of his property, and if any one attempted to do so the owner could obtain an injunction, compelling him to remove the obstruction. All Governments ever since Confederation have favoured granting foreshore rights to people who own the land facing the water, provided they required the foreshore for the purposes of improvement.

My hon. friend is perfectly correct in stating that the two departments co-operate in fixing the price. Would my hon. friend accept the valuation of the Chief Engineer of the Marine and Fisheries Department in signing his report?

The practice with me was always this: There would come to my department a report signed by the chief engineer of the Marine and Fisheries Department, and a recommendation to council signed by the minister, and I wouln accept the report of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries as to valuation.
Inasmuch as my hon. friend had to sign these reports in regard to this property which was given by Order in Council for $180, and two years afterwards sold for $600,000-
Was that a sale?

An absolute sale. The Crown grant was made, and the sale took
place from John Hendry to the British Columbia Electric.
Did Mr. Hendry sell all the riparian rights as well in that transfer?
It was foreshore, which included riparian rights.
If it was solely foreshore how could they get access to it except by water?

It was exactly the same property that my hon. friend gave for $180. I wish to ask a second question. If my hon. friend accepts the valuation of the chief engineer of the Marine and Fisheries Department, why did he override at that time the valuation of $180,000 fixed by Colonel Anderson, chief engineer of the Marine and Fisheries Department, and sell the land for $10 an acre, or $180.
The answer to that is I do not believe I did anything of the kind.
I will bring down the papers to-morrow.
I wish my hon. friend would. I am satisfied he is entirely mistaken.
I am positive I am right.

With regard to the sale which Hendry may have made to the British Columbia Electric, I venture to say he sold not only the foreshore, but a large area of land fronting on the water, which of course would include riparian rights in the foreshore. The remark which my hon friend has made with regard to property being sold to this Government for $360,000 reminds me of rumours which I have heard from Vancouver, that certain friends of my hon. friend the member for the city of Vancouver had succeeded in getting an enormous sum from this Government for a property which was worth very much less than the Government paid for it. That perhaps accounts for the rumours I have also heard that certain gentlemen received large commissions in connection with the transfer of that property.
What property does niy hon. friend refer to?
The property is said to have cost $360,000, and the rumours I have heard reflect very seriously upon my hon. friend and friends of his.

As my hon. friend has brought that matter up, I will tell him that the dock site in Vancouver was chosen by engineers of the department without any interference whatsoever; and what property did they chose? Did they go to friends of this Government? No, they bought a piece of property belonging to Mr. Robert Kelly and Mr. McFeely, two of the most prominent Liberals in Vancouver. How did they buy it? Not as my hon. friend has no doubt done, by means of a nice private transaction between the department and the owner. No, they took it to the Exchequer Court. There was absolutely no middleman of any kind whatsoever, and I defy my hon. friend to produce one scintilla of evidence to show that there was even a middleman, let alone him getting anything out of it. The matter was not settled even by arbitration, but was taken to the Exchequer Court, and as the award was not satisfactory to Kelly and McFeely, the case was appealed. My hon. friend has no right to insinuate that there is anything in the transaction reflecting upon me unless he is in possession of facts to prove it. The facts that I have given can be proved beyond all peradven-ture by Order in Council. Yet the hon. member presumes to stand up in his place and throw out what I consider the contemptible insinuation that I was mixed up in the transaction, and that I or friends of mine profited by it.
I again challenge him and defy him to produce one scintilla of evidence to show that there was even a middleman in the property, let alone any commission. He knows, if he knows anything about it at all, that what he says is absolutely without the slightest foundation in fact.

The hon. gentleman says I have no ground for the suggestion I made, and that neither Ihe nor his friends were interested. If he knows that I gladly accept his word. The statement on which I was relying was contained in a letter which I received from Vancouver, in which reference was made to-
Will the hon. gentleman give me the name of the writer? Will he give it to the committee?-or to Mr. Speaker?-or to the Prime Minister?

I was speaking from memory. Tihe letter was received by me last year or the year before. Whether I have it on file now or not I do not know. But the statement in that letter is corroborated by the statement of the hon.

gentleman himself that these gentlemen paid something like $3,000 for a property for which they received from this Government the princely sum of $360,000.
Under award of the Exchequer Court.	,

These awards depend largely upon the counsel engaged and the witnesses called to give information to the judge. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Stevens) is too old a bird not to understand how these things are done. He may smile, but I think he knows how these things are done -with friendly counsel and friends all around who are not desirous of making too hard a bargain. The hon. gentleman speaks of Mr. Robert Kelly. Mr. Kelly is a very fine fellow; indeed, one of the best men in the city of Vancouver. But I have yet to learn that if Mr. Kelly had a property he wanted to sell to the Dominion Government, say for a wharf site, he would be averse to availing himself of the assistance of friends in representing the value of that property to the Government. I do not know that that would be a serious reflection upon his standing or reputation. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Stevens) has said that there was no middleman-
Absolutely none.

If he says that there
was none, and that his friends were not interested, and that the Government agents first approached Mr. Kelly, or whoever owned the property, in the ordinary business way, and the case was tried out bona fide, and the full evidence presented, and that the Government got the land at a fair valuation, I am prepared to accept his statement.
And Mr. Kelly and his associates were dissatisfied with the award of the Exchequer Court.

I do not see why they should be greatly dissatisfied in view of the fact that for a property for which they paid $3,000 they got $360,000. Gentlemen in the part of the country from which I come would be greatly pleased with such a transaction. What was the frontage?

About 350 feet, so far as their particular part was concerned. Let me correct my hon. friend-he has had iquite a, little spell at it now, let me put in a moment's correction. Because the hon. gentleman has peculiar ability in misleading the House somewhat in matters of fact. Let me remind him that it wag he who

signed the Order in Council together with the head of the Marine Department in. the Government of which he was a member, which gave this property to his friends for the remarkably low sum of $3,600. If any crime against public right was committed, the guilt lies at the door of the late Government. The value placed upon the property by the Exchequer Court was a fair value. But these gentlemen had a Crown grant from-his Government, and it is the price that Government accepted on behalf of the people of Canada to which I was calling the attention of the Committee, and to which attention should be called. He is not going to get away from it by trying to slip it around to the allegation that the present Government paid more than it ought to have paid. They paid what the Exchequer Court awarded, after a hearing that was bitterly fought out.
The foreshore, the hon. gentleman says, was 350 feet. How much of that is actually occupied by any wharf, building, or other structures?
There was an old mill.
What was the depth of the property from high water to low water':
He is not going to get me tangled up in matters of that kind. The foreshore sold by his Government-

I am asking now about what was sold to this Government.
Mr. STEVEN'S: The hon. gentleman is not trying to find out the facts, 'but is trying to make the matter appear an involved one to the members of the committee and to Hansard. His Government presented Mr. Kelly and Mr. McFeely a property from high tide mark out beyond low tide mark- 1 have forgotten the exact distance, but I think it was 700 feet-for $3,600. From high tide mark to the inner boundary of the property was a comparatively sh.ort distance.
What distance?

It varies, as it was a
kind of a hay. It might be 100 feet.
What was the distance between high tide and low tide?
That had nothing to do with it, because it was not from high tide to low tide, but he gave from high tide 600 feet put and beyond low tide.

If any one is trying to mislead the committee, it is the hon. gentleman (Mr. Stevens), unless he is speaking in ignorance of the law. He ought to know that no Government could give Mr. Kelly or any one else rights beyond low tide, for that is common to the whole world; it does not belong to the Crown, and I venture to say that this Government neveT undertook to grant it. If Mr. Kelly built out into the navigable harbour, he had no right to do so. I understand now that he built out about 600 feet.

No, I said that the area covered by the Crown grant recommended by the hon. gentleman in his report to council and iby his associate the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries was approximately 600 feet.
The hon. gentleman said it went put beyond low water mark.
Certainly.

I say it could not do so, because the Crown has no right beyond low water mark. He says that in addition to these rights Mr. Kelly and his associates owned the riparian rights as well, and that these were sold to this Government in conjunction with the foreshore. There is the difference. The foreshore right is practically of no value whatever as distinct from the rights pf the riparian owner, because the riparian owner could prevent any obstruction being placed in the foreshore; but with the two holding together he has something that he can dispose of as a joint property. The hon. gentleman will Tecognize that he is the one who has tried to deceive the committee because the foreshore rights acquired from the Government for about $3,000 were sold to the present Government for $360,000.
He now says that in addition to the foreshore rights, Mr. Kelly and his associates owned the riparian rights, the whole of which, with certain improvements upon the property, were passed over to the Dominion Government. That is all I have to say. I am sorry to have taken up the time and I would not have done so had it not been fox my hon. friend digressing in order to make it appear that the Liberal Government had parted with that property in Vancouver for less than it was worth.

I am sorry to have to delay the committee, but it is so seldom that a statement such as I made finds such exact corroboration from the other side of the House as my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) was good enough to



give me this evening that I cannot help but draw attention to it. We find ourselves in absolute agreement on almost all important points. He is just as certain as I am that the absolute right to the Indian reserves in British Columbia Tests in the Indians and is absolutely under the jurisdiction of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs. He explains to the committee, and I entirely agree with him, the ostensible principle under which the then mittee. But they claimed the absolute right to all abandoned reserves. If they could secure the abandonment of this reserve, they would become its owners, and so they employed agents to deal with the Indians to secure that abandonment to the end that they might become the absolute owners. Now, we are absolutely in agreement upon this line of facts and there is no argument about the matter. We disagree when he says that the then Superintendent General of Indian Affairs in any way contested the action of the British Columbia Government at that time or in any way undertook to protect the interests of the Indians or the rights of this Government as protecting the Indians. He declares to the committee that this Government, through its Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, did everything it could to protect the Indians against this attack upon their rights, which he has described so accurately. He will remember that when this transaction was actually in progress, it was ventilated in the Vancouver papers from day to day and that at was brought by myself to the attention of the then Superintendent General of Indian Affairs. It was therefore absolutely within his cognizance. My hon. friend from Vancouver assures the House that it was absolutely within has jurisdiction and the facts as recorded in the Vancouver papers, and the facts as they occurred, are that the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs did not then or afterwards take any action to prevent this carefully planned, determinedly made and concerted attack upon the rights of the Indians. He admitted so much that there is no use in his attempting to deny what is such a patent fact. With regard to the remarks of my hon. friend as to my connection with the matter, I certainly say that I was approached on numerous occasions to secure the surrender of- the Kitsilano reserve. I took such measures as were possible to secure its surrender, and if my memory serves me aright, I found difficulties in the way. The legislation which was the subject of discussion between the Minister of the Interior and myself this evening, .was brought into Parliament and put through under my auspices for the especial purpose of dealing with the Kitsilano Indian reserve. However, the people of Canada kindly took the responsibility out of my hands and I was not further concerned in it. That is my connection with the Indian reserve and I can assure my hon. friend that whatever any supporter of the Liberal Government may have said in Vancouver-and I would not like to be responsible for everything that everybody in Vancouver might say-he never had any authority from me to say that any such disposition would be made of the Kitsilano reserve when the rights of the Indians in that reserve had been disposed of.
I shall not delay the committee further than to point out that the set of facts that I have placed before the committee has been absolutely substantiated by my hon. friend from Vancouver who was on the ground and is familiar with the circumstances. There certainly has been a change of policy on the part of this Government from the time when they did consent, and must have consented, to the transaction of the provincial government with these Indians on the basis of $300,000 and it is interesting to compare that policy with t'he policy of to-day which refuses $660,000 as a fair price for the reserve. My hon. friend has told the House that the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs had said that the provincial government would be recouped for the money they had spent.
